title: Federal Court rules against challenge to SA government's golf course plans
text:
Two South Australians have failed in a bid to stop the felling of trees as part of the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera brought the action against the State Government in the Federal Court earlier this year arguing that the redevelopment was in breach of federal conservation laws.

The Federal Court trial heard last month that 400 trees had been cut down to date, with the government previously saying 585 would ultimately go.

The court also today lifted a temporary injunction put in place to stop the works for the duration of the court case, meaning construction can now recommence.

Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera have 28 days to file an appeal against the decision.

title: Chris Fagan headed the ultimate Lions reawakening
text:
Chris Fagan said earlier this week: "You don't coach a team to win a popularity contest."

Despite his best intentions, the departing Brisbane Lions three-time premiership winning coach has done just that.

Today, after days of speculation, the 65-year-old has told the club he he will step down.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life," he said.

"We have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that."

In his decade at the Lions, Fagan has broken the mould of what is needed to be an AFL coach. He also leaves as one of the most popular figures in Australian sport.

The reason Fagan took on the difficult job at the Lions back in 2016 was to help the club on its road to redemption.

Safe to say now, a little more than 10 years on, mission accomplished.

Three AFL premierships. In a row.

Chris Fagan and the Brisbane Lions celebrate their third consecutive AFL premiership. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer/AFL Photos)

Fagan is also known as "Fages", or "Papa Fages" to so many of the young men he coached during his tenure. Many have referred to him as a father figure, or another grandfather.

That respect goes both ways, with Fagan often noting that he considered players at the club as his sons, and wanted to "help them develop into the best people they can be".

He finishes his role with 148 wins in 243 games as head coach, the most of any Brisbane Lions coach of all time, and of course those three titles.

Brisbane will never forget the work, effort and glory he has given the team.

But back in October 2016, public opinion on the surprise appointment was mixed.

A goalscoring teacher

Fagan grew up in Queenstown, Tasmania — a far cry from the humidity of Brisbane.

He played 260 games of senior footy in the Tasmanian Football League with Hobart, Sandy Bay and Devonport between 1978 and 1990.

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan, third from the left at the front, grew up in Queenstown and played for the Lyell-Gormanston football club as a junior. (Supplied: Galley Museum Collection)

Before coaching, Fagan went into teaching, working as a high school teacher in Tasmania towards the end of his playing career. He took on some local coaching roles in Tasmania.

The long apprenticeship from high school teacher to three-peat AFL premiership winning coach began in 1999 when AFL great Neale Daniher brought him to Melbourne Football Club.

He served under Daniher until 2007 before joining as an assistant and eventually general manager of football at Hawthorn.

The Lions hierarchy saw the value in what Fagan had learned and appointed him to replace Justin Leppitsch in late 2016.

Fresh start for Brisbane

After finishing second bottom of the ladder in 2016, the Brisbane Lions were looking for a fresh start.

A five-person coaching selection panel, led by then club chief executive Greg Swann, made the selection to appoint Fagan on October 4.

Chris Fagan speaks to the media after being unveiled as the Brisbane Lions' coach in 2016. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

The committee said Fagan was "exactly the person" the club needed.

"Chris is the perfect fit for the Brisbane Lions as we strive to regain relevance — his knowledge, experience, mentoring skills and ability to communicate are all elite," Swann said announcing the appointment.

At the time, Fagan said he felt Brisbane's best football was ahead of them.

Yet in Fagan's first season at the club, the Lions finished rock bottom. The team ended the 2017 campaign with 17 losses.

The Brisbane Lions lost 19 of 22 games in 2016, finishing second-last on the ladder. (AAP: Ben Macmahon)

You would be forgiven if you thought Fagan must have been disheartened after his first season at the club ending in a wooden spoon.

You would also be wrong.

"It's been a great year, I've learned so much about the group," Fagan said in August 2017.

"I think right now, I'm in a good position to know what's required."

Lions coach Chris Fagan (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The 'Gabbatoir' returns

In 2019, Fagan took the Lions to second on the ladder and a semifinal.

They narrowly lost the semifinal to Greater Western Sydney, but it was a marked turnaround from the year prior.

It had been a long time since playing in Brisbane was seen as a difficult away trip, but that year Fagan and his Lions turned the Gabba into a fortress.

Chris Fagan and the Lions turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". (Getty Images: Albert Perez/AFL Photos)

From 2019 to 2023 the Lions won 49 of 53 regular season games at the Gabba. In 2023, Brisbane were unbeaten at home.

Once again, the Lions had turned the Gabba into the "Gabbatoir". He had made them believe.

"There's nothing magical or mysterious about it," he said in 2019 before the incredible home form began, adding the secret would be hard work, staying humble and believing.

He led the club to the Finals series in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022.

At the end of the 2022 season, Fagan took a leave of absence as Brisbane coach to assist with an external review into the treatment of Indigenous players during his time as an employee at Hawthorn alongside then-coach Alastair Clarkson and former welfare manager Jason Burt.

Fagan, Clarkson and Burt categorically denied all allegations of wrongdoing, and the case was settled out of court. Fagan returned to his coaching duties in late October 2022.

In 2023, he guided the Lions to their first grand final in 19 years. They lost to Collingwood by four points.

Despite the frustrations of falling at the final hurdle, Fagan asked the fans and his players to be patient.

Fagan shakes hands with Collingwood coach Craig McRae after the Lions' grand final loss in 2023. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Daniel Pockett)

"Grand final losses don't have to define you or destroy you, they can make you," he said.

"There's lots of teams in the history of the game that have lost close grand finals and gone on to win premierships in the ensuing years."

Almost as if he knew.

Back-to-back-to-back

In 2024, after a fifth-placed finish in the regular season, the Lions clawed their way through the longer finals path to reach the grand final.

In it, they defeated the Sydney Swans 120-60 in what was an emphatic victory. They became just the third team to win the premiership from outside the top four.

Brisbane Lions players and coach Chris Fagan after winning the 2024 grand final against the Sydney Swans. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"I'm so proud of the group, the resilience that they've shown this year," Fagan told ABC Sport after the win.

"We certainly know how to do it the hard way, but it makes it all that better when you achieve it."

He was right about Lions doing things the hard way. In 2025 the Lions lost their qualifying final against Geelong, 112-74.

Despite that, the Lions eased past Gold Coast Suns in the semifinal and then defeated Collingwood in the preliminary final, setting up a rematch against Geelong in the grand final.

The Lions turned around the qualifying final result and defeated Geelong 122-75 to claim their second premiership in as many years.

Self belief within the group was at an all time high going into the match, Fagan recalled afterwards.

"I always talked about the idea of failing our way to the top," Fagan said after becoming a back-to-back premiership winner.

“We don’t get too upset when we lose. I think everybody has embraced that at the footy club."

Harris Andrews, Chris Fagan and Lachie Neale celebrate the Lions' 2025 victory. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

The 2026 season saw the Lions defeated in the qualifying final once again. This time the Swans humbled Brisbane 144-88.

Brisbane had to do it the hard way for the third year in a row. "We've got work to do," Fagan said.

In the post match conference he posed a question to his players: "How badly do they want it? We'll see."

It turned out they wanted it (a three-peat) badly. The Lions roared past Adelaide Crows, then held off Hawthorn on the way to a fourth consecutive grand final.

In that final, against Fremantle, the Lions pulled off what can only be described as unbelievable to claim their third AFL premiership in a row.

With a little over four minutes left on the clock they trailed by 17 points. The camera panned to Fagan on the sideline, he looked his usual calm self. He believed.

As did his players, just like he had asked them to do for the last 10 years. Believe.

Against the run of play and all logic, the Lions scored four unanswered goals as the clock ran down and won the match by seven points in an instant classic.

Fagan leaves the Lions at the peak of his powers. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Fagan had coached the players to have so much belief in themselves that they would produce results where no one else would think possible. But under Fagan's stewardship it was.

Until his achievements with the Lions, successful AFL coaches had all played at the top level, and typically utilised old school methods of rallying the troops.

But Fagan's coaching ethos has relied on mutual trust, relationships and emotional intelligence to challenge his players. Now, he walks out on top.

Never someone to chase personal accolades, Fagan is leaving the role at the peak of his powers, and opting not to chase the four-peat that would leave him in even rarer air.

Fagan took on one of AFL's biggest assignments at the Lions and leaves a club favourite. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

It was one of the AFL's biggest assignments — saving a flagship club that was depleted on and off the field. Brisbane was not only struggling to win matches, the club was also losing memberships and crowds.

Fast forward to the end of the 2026 season, and Chris Fagan has finished that assignment.

He passed with flying (maroon, blue and gold) colours.

title: From tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle has gone 'Knights crazy'
text:
It's been 25 years since the Newcastle Knights last played in an NRL grand final, and Newcastle has not forgotten how to celebrate.

From fresh tattoos to blue sausages, the city is going all out ahead of the decider against the Sydney Roosters on Sunday.

Tattoo artist Dave Ross cancelled all his appointments this week to make space for footy fans itching to get one of his limited-edition Knights tattoos.

"It's just been insane, like nothing I could ever imagine," he said.

Local tattoo artist Dave Ross says he is fully booked out with Newcastle Knights fans lining up to get commemorative tattoos. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

"I get to spend the week tattooing Knights designs on all these diehard fans … it's been incredible."

Fifteen more tattoos have been booked in for later this week, with Mr Ross staying back until 9pm to get them done.

Lifelong supporter Sam Mawer decided to get a tattoo after the team made it to the grand final.

Sam Mawer got a tattoo with the Knights' slogan: "Defend the kingdom." (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

"I'm a Knights tragic … I didn't think we would happen again in my lifetime," he said.

"I'm getting it on the back of my calf so I can look down every now and then and hopefully have fond memories of the grand final."

On the cusp of their first premiership in 25 years, local tattoo shops have jumped on the Newcastle Knights bandwagon. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Armidale man Dave Battese got inked live on the radio to win tickets to the Knights' last grand final match against the Parramatta Eels in 2001.

"People were cringing because you could literally hear the tattoo gun bouncing on my skull," he said.

"I was making jokes about how this is nothing [compared] to the pain that Newcastle are going to put on Parramatta."

Dave Battese says he's proudly worn his Knights tattoos for 25 years. (Supplied: Dave Battese)

Mr Battese said he's proudly displayed his tattoos for 25 years, including through five wooden spoon seasons, and hopes he can add a fresh tattoo this year to celebrate a third premiership.

Blue and red food

Other Newcastle businesses have jumped on the bandwagon, including a butcher creating a blue sausage.

"It's a pork sausage and just added a little bit of food dye," manager Johnny Emeny said.

"We just wanted to get behind our mighty boys as they get to this grand final and no better way than throwing a few blue sausages on the barbecue," he said.

Johnny Emeny says he enjoys getting creative by making blue sausages. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

" The whole town has just gone Knights crazy. "

Since Monday, homes and businesses across the Hunter have been painted red and blue in support of the team.

Other Knights-themed foods like blue burgers in pubs and blue-and-red ice cream have also popped up around town.

A Newcastle pub is selling a blue burger with red sauce to support the Knights. (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

The original Knight

Like many Novocastrians, Cliff Parker remembers exactly where he was when the Knights won their first grand final in 1997.

Dressed in a suit of shining armour, Mr Parker and his trusty horse Rocky led the Knights team bus back through the city after their win against Manly.

Loading...

"It was absolutely mad … I could not believe the amount of people lining the streets," Mr Parker said.

"I was riding up and down in the crowd, and they were going nuts."

For 25 years, Cliff Parker was the Newcastle Knights' mascot on horseback at the team's home games. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

For 25 years, Mr Parker and Rocky were the team's mascot, the Newcastle Knight, riding along the sidelines at home games to hype up the crowd before kick-off.

But no-one ever knew the identity of the mysterious armoured crusader.

"No-one ever knew me as Cliff by name," said Mr Parker.

"Rocky was definitely the more famous one."

Sammy Pistolas wears the original suit that his dad, Chris Kelly, wore as the Newcastle Knights' mascot, Sir Rusty. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Another iconic mascot at Knights home games was Sir Rusty, portrayed by Chris Kelly.

"Dad would ride around the ground on a quad bike as Sir Rusty and have fun with the crowd … just goofing off," Mr Kelly's son, Sammy Pistolas, said.

For this final, Mr Pistolas is supporting the team by tattooing Knights fans in the original Sir Rusty costume.

"I think my Mum made it … the body piece is from the 1997 grand final, and the head piece is from the 2001 grand final," he said.

title: Doctors and allied health professionals to walk off job en masse amid pay disputes
text:
Doctors and allied health professionals at Victoria's public hospitals have walked off the job today, as year-long bargaining processes with the government over pay and conditions remain at a standstill.

Doctors across the state will undertake a four-hour work stoppage from 3:30pm to 7:30pm, while allied health professionals will strike for a full 24 hours.

Hospital emergency departments will be excluded from the work stoppage, with staffing across hospitals remaining at Saturday levels to protect patient safety and welfare.

The Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association (VAHPA) said exemptions to the stop work would apply in certain sectors such as emergency care, neo-natal, maternity and paediatric patients, and units with high dependency patients such as oncology, coronary and palliative care to ensure patients are not affected.

Government negotiations with both doctors and allied health professionals have dragged on for more than a year without a resolution. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

The Australian Medical Association's (AMA) Victorian branch president Simon Judkins said today's protest by doctors came as a last resort following "over 60 meetings and six months of promises that an offer was imminent".

"Doctors do not want to be attending protests. They want to be in their hospitals doing what they've dedicated their lives to, and that's caring for their patients," Dr Judkins said.

"But the reality is, they cannot do that job properly and safely with the unsustainable working conditions and staffing the government has provided."

Allied health professionals in units with high patients dependency such as oncology and maternity units will be exempt from the strike. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

Dr Judkins said the AMA was calling for conditions consistent with other emergency services, including a 12.5-hour cap on shifts and guarantee of three consecutive days off during a fortnight of work.

Government yet to put deal on table, doctor's union says

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said the government was speaking with the AMA about its concerns, and hoped both parties would reach a resolution soon.

"Those discussions are progressing well and I'm absolutely focused on making sure that they result in a settlement that everybody is comfortable with," Ms Stitt said.

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

Ms Stitt said strong plans were in place to ensure patient safety during the strike, and confirmed hours of work and doctor fatigue formed part of the discussions.

However, the health minister could not confirm if the government had made any offers in the past 14 months, and the AMA said no offer had yet been received from the government.

The doctors strike coincides with a 24-hour strike by allied health professionals, who are yet to secure a deal with the government after 12 months of negotiations.

The government says discussions are continuing with union officials today. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

Members of VAHPA, which represents professions such as radiographers, physiotherapists and social workers, have gone on strike at 43 public sector hospitals in the state.

VAHPA secretary Aneta Menkinoska said Victorian allied health professionals were among the worst paid in the country.

"Highly experienced clinicians are leaving the workforce due to burnout and unreasonable workloads. It's not sustainable," she said.

"Poor pay means we cannot retain and attract staff to fill the gaps. Why would you bother getting a four-year degree to be paid so poorly?"

title: Chris Fagan steps down from Brisbane Lions
text:
Chris Fagan has told the Brisbane Lions he is stepping down as coach following the club's third-straight AFL premiership success.

The 65-year-old led Brisbane to a stunning 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) victory against Fremantle on Saturday.

However, he told the club he wanted to step away from the final year of his contract to be closer to his family.

"I've been thinking about this for some time and I'm comfortable that now is the right time for [my wife] Ursula and I to return to Melbourne," Fagan said in a statement.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life.

"Together, we have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that.

"I was grateful to be given the role to coach the club, and it has been an incredible ride.

"This job is all-encompassing; I've given it my absolute all and I'm so proud of what we've achieved, but now is the right time to go."

Fagan coached the Lions to the second premiership three-peat in the club's history. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Fagan took charge of the Lions in 2017, and leaves having coached 243 games with a winning record of 61.32 per cent.

This year, he passed legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews as having coached the most games for the club.

The former school teacher was also part of the Hawthorn coaching staff as the club also won a three-peat of flags from 2013–2015 as well playing a role in their 2008 triumph.

In total, Fagan led the Lions in eight-straight finals series after claiming the wooden spoon in his opening season, winning just five games in each of his first two seasons.

Saturday's stunning come-from-behind triumph was the Lions' third-successive victory in a decider after beating Sydney and Geelong over the past two years.

He also led the Lions to the 2023 grand final, falling four points short of Collingwood.

Fagan speaking to his Lions players during his first season in charge. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Brisbane Lions chair Andrew Wellington hailed Fagan for his "unwavering commitment" to helping others achieve their goals.

"Chris arrived at our club with a clear view of what good people, strong relationships and shared belief could achieve," Wellington said.

"His influence has reached far beyond the Brisbane Lions. Chris has helped strengthen football across Queensland, inspired a new generation of players and supporters, and earned the respect of the wider football public for the way he has carried himself through success and adversity."

Chief executive Sam Graham said the club respected Fagan's decision and that steps would be taken to appoint a new coach "in due course".

"Chris has played a massive role in the transformation of this club both on and off the field," he said.

"While we would have loved nothing more for him to continue on, he has earned the right to call time when he was ready, and we're pleased he's going out on top.

"Chris's achievements speak for themselves, but his greatest legacy is the environment he created, the people he developed and how he has nurtured this playing group."

Leigh Mathews (left) congratulates Chris Fagan after Saturday's grand final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Darrian Traynor)

His departure means the Lions will have to look for a new coach to help a stacked playing list attempt to win the first AFL/VFL four-peat since the Collingwood team of 1927–30.

Possible internal candidates include Brisbane's football boss Danny Daly, senior assistant coach Cameron Bruce or backline coach Dale Morris.

Former league head coaches Nathan Buckley, Adam Simpson and Simon Goodwin have also been proposed as possible replacements.

"This club has never been in greater shape, and the list profile would suggest this," Fagan said.

"The boys will continue to contend, and I'll be their number-one fan, but a fresh face at the helm will be a key pillar for the players to come back to next season as they work hard to achieve more success.

"I'll miss the club and it will feel strange not to be involved, but for the last 10 years I've thought about nothing other than how we can improve, get better and be successful.

"To see the club develop on field from cellar dwellers to three-time premiers has been amazing.

"The Lions are the sum of our parts and everyone across the club has played their role."

title: Labor MPs jockey for position on election tickets as party braces for losses
text:
Labor will not have upper house candidates locked in until one month before the Victorian election, leaving senior ministers in political purgatory, as the party grapples with the prospect of losing almost half its MPs in the chamber.

Labor currently holds 15 seats in the 40-member chamber, but dire polling has the party bracing for major losses.

While the party currently has two MPs in all regions except one, Labor expects almost all its candidates in the number two position on their ballots will be turfed out at the election.

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

In this scenario, Labor's representation in the upper house would be reduced to just nine MPs.

Factional groupings have been thrashing out deals to protect and prioritise MPs in losing positions, dragging out the process and frustrating MPs unsure of their candidacy.

Senior ministers Ingrid Stitt and Enver Erdogan both currently hold the second position in their regions.

A deal hashed out in an attempt to spare Mr Erdogan has angered local members, who are petitioning the party to retain their existing MP.

Enver Erdogan has served as member for Northern Metropolitan Region since 2022. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

An "indicative timeline", due to be approved by the party's administrative committee tonight, confirmed preselections for positions currently held by Labor will be decided by the national executive on October 21.

The remaining seats will be determined a week later, one month before the November 28 election and just a few days before the government enters caretaker mode, according to the timeline obtained by the ABC.

Some MPs have privately complained of being kept out of the loop, leaving them wondering whether they should be investing in their campaign.

"It's completely disrespectful and contemptible to treat sitting [members of the Legislative Council] in this way," one source said on condition of anonymity.

Handshake agreement sends senior minister to safer position

The ABC has confirmed with several sources that a handshake agreement will move Mr Erdogan to the safer top position in Eastern Victoria, which covers Gippsland.

The existing MP there, Tom McIntosh, will take Mr Erdogan's position as the second candidate in the Northern Metro.

Tom McIntosh may be moved from his current seat to give Enver Erdogan a better chance at remaining in parliament. (Supplied)

Labor is hopeful of retaining two MPs in that electorate, which covers the inner-north and stretches to the outskirts of the northern suburbs, though it is less secure than his existing top spot for Labor in Eastern Victoria.

The two MPs are from separate subgroups within Labor's broader Right faction, which are blocs of members and powerbrokers who share allegiances.

The ABC contacted the MPs on Thursday.

Sonny Stephens, Labor's candidate in the lower house seat Gippsland East, in August launched a petition to keep Mr McIntosh in the top position in Eastern Victoria. Three hundred members signed her petition, which she will send to the national executive on Thursday night.

Sonny Stephens says Labor members feel disappointed with the decisions. (Supplied)

Ms Stephens told the ABC that Mr McIntosh was hardworking and a "stunningly good politician".

She said she had heard from members a "frustration with a process that doesn't appear to reward effort".

"The emotion that a decision like this generates among the members is just a terrible thing. It's not what you want in the run-up to the election," Ms Stephens said.

"People feel disappointed. They feel powerless. Hopefully the petition is one way they can vent their frustration."

title: Forrester breaks 17yo record at short course titles
text:
Jenna Forrester's outstanding 2026 has continued at the Australian Short Course Championships in Sydney, lowering the Australian women's 400m individual medley record on her way to gold.

The 23-year-old beat Ellen Fullerton's 17-year-old mark with a time of 4:28.39, taking 0.33 seconds off the record.

The time was comfortably under the qualifying standard for the upcoming world championships in Beijing.

Remarkably, Forrester had only just competed in the 200 backstroke, finishing second to Iona Anderson, also swimming under the qualification time for Beijing.

Iona Anderson held on to beat a fast-finishing Forrester in the 200m backstroke. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"That was a shock. I came here with no expectations, just to jump in and have a bit of fun," Forrester said after the race.

"I haven't done a lot of short course and that hurt doubling up [with the 200m backstroke] but I've done a lot of double-ups, especially internationally."

Forrester has already had a year to remember in 2026, claiming three individual gold medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in the 200m backstroke, 200m IM and 400m IM, as well as winning bronze in the 400m freestyle.

She also won silver in the 400m IM at the Pan Pacs in California behind Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh.

Just 24 athletes will be selected for the team that will head to China and the famous Water Cube from December 1-6 — and Forrester has put her hand up to be one of them.

"I've always wanted to represent Australia at [the World] short course," Forrester said.

"Hopefully this year is my year."

Anderson, who also claimed four medals at the Commonwealth Games, including gold in the 100m backstroke and silver in the 50m, did her chances of selection no harm by claiming her second title of the meet.

Southam delivers statement win

In the men's 100m freestyle, Commonwealth Games champ Flynn Southam cruised to victory with a rapid 45.61.

"It's good to back up after Comm Games and be consistent but it's been pretty hard to stay motivated," Southam said.

"I'm pretty stoked with that time, to be honest … bring on the World Champs."

The 21-year-old Bond swimmer was a scratching from the 200m freestyle on the opening night to focus on the four-length dash, and he duly delivered, beating Ed Sommerville into silver by 0.45 seconds.

Flynn Southam is eyeing up the world championships in Beijing. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Southam, who won gold in the 4x50m freestyle relay at the 2022 short course worlds in Melbourne, as well as picking up three relay silvers and a bronze, said is ready to make the jump to claim an individual medal in Beijing.

"The last time I raced short course was the worlds in Melbourne four years ago so I'm really looking forward to racing the big dogs," he said.

"Comm Games was a good taste test for me with Matt Richards [Wales] and obviously Kyle [Chalmers].

"I know David Popovici [Romania's Olympic 200m champion] isn't doing worlds but Jack Alexy [USA] is someone else on my list who I'm looking forward to racing.

"As for expectation — bring on the pressure. Sometimes it does make me nervous, but I love it, and I breathe it."

Olivia Wunsch claimed the 100m free by almost a second and a half in a dominant performance. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the women's 100m free, Olivia Wunsch needed a personal best of 51.72 to beat Lani Pallister into silver.

The 20-year-old led from the gun to power away from the field, beating distance specialist Pallister by a colossal 1.46 seconds.

"It was pretty special to go under 52 for the first time. Doing 52 at World Cups last year was nice, but I think I surprised myself a little bit off the sort of short prep I've had into short course," Wunsch said.

"I had about three weeks off in total … it's been nice to just get back in the water, swim a little bit less, and just focus on getting my speed and enjoying getting back into it."

Rowan Crothers claimed a second victory of the week following his world record on Tuesday. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the men's multiclass 50m freestyle, Rowan Crothers equalled his national record to beat S10 rival Alex Tuckwell into silver.

"I'm blessed to be Australian and to have the chance to race the best in the world over and over again at these meets … watch this space because we'll be sharing a podium in LA," Tuckfield said.

Two-time Paralympic champion Crothers simply said it was "bloody exciting" to see how fast his 21-year-old rival was going.

title: Fake news and deepfakes about flydubai flight spreading online
text:
In the hours since the mid-air incident aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, false information and fake video have been circulating widely on social media.

In the modern news environment, major events can often be targets for people wanting to spread false narratives or "go viral" with dramatic — and bogus — details.

Add in the tense geopolitics of the regions involved in this particular incident and you have all the ingredients required for a misinformation perfect storm.

ABC NEWS Verify has examined and attempted to debunk some of the fake news that's spreading online.

False flag incident was 'staged' by Israel

Rumours started spreading quickly and widely in the wake of this incident that it was an Israeli-planned event, with one tweet by popular United States conspiracy theorist Jackson Hinkle being viewed on X more than 1.5 million times.

A post on X by popular US conspiracy theorist Jackson Hinkle. (X)

Multiple other posts describing the midair incident as a "false flag" operation — or an act disguising the true person or party responsible — have also been shared widely.

Given that the investigation into the incident is only hours old and the motivation and history of the alleged perpetrator is still unknown, this narrative appears to be relying on anti-Zionist and anti-Semitic tropes rather than any established facts.



The source of this post, Jackson Hickle, has a reported history of spreading falsehoods, an act that may be financially incentivised as he's previously admitted to receiving payments from X.com in exchange for highly engaging posts.

BBC deepfake

This deepfake video purporting to be a real BBC News report was posted onto X just a couple of hours after the incident.

A deepfake video purporting to be from the BBC. (X)

It appears to have been created using real footage of BBC presenter Sally Bundock, but AI-manipulated with a fake Australian voice and script.

The deepfake combines footage of a plane flying over a city that appears to be completely unrelated to this flydubai incident, as well as real verified video from inside the flight.

It's pushing a narrative that Indian officials were somehow involved in the incident alongside Mossad — something there is simply no established evidence for.

The post has been viewed more than 300,000 times but does now have an added content note on X that describes it as "AI slop".

What's notable is how quickly it was produced, and how realistic elements of it are, including the reproduction of BBC News visual signposts and the use of a real presenter's face and body.

Anti-Pakistan and anti-Indian sentiment

Multiple posts about the "true" nationality or citizenship of the pilot responsible have been spread on social media, well before any established information about his identity or alleged motivation had been formally released by authorities.

An X post made after the incident. (X)

While the "hero" pilot has been publicly identified by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as Indian pilot captain Smit Machchhar, no official information about the alleged perpetrator had been made publicly available when these posts went out, and they appear to rely entirely on anti-Pakistani sentiment.

Reuters has since reported that an unnamed Israeli official had identified the attacker as an Omani national.

Ongoing tensions between Pakistan and India have become a motivation for some accounts seeking to spread misinformation aimed at blaming major events on Pakistani or Indian nationals — something that was also seen after the Bondi massacre.

ABC NEWS Verify recommends always examining the sources of material being spread online, asking yourself questions about their motivation and legitimacy and always looking for corroboration from trusted news providers.

title: Man City could face fines, EPL expulsion, over financial rules scandal
text:
Manchester City faces an uncertain future after the decorated English soccer club was found guilty of systematically breaking the Premier League's financial rules for nearly a decade.

The verdict, delivered by an independent disciplinary commission, leaves open an array of sanctions, including a fine, points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League.

City could also face possible compensation claims from rival teams, while its ownership — the Abu Dhabi-controlled City Football Group — is coming under increasing scrutiny.

The club has rejected the verdict in a case that dates to 2018 and mainly covers its financial dealings from 2009 to 2018, and promises a relentless campaign to clear its name.

Here's a look at what's next in one of the biggest scandals in English soccer history.

Loading...

City promises 'relentless' challenge to the verdict

City can appeal the verdict and has insisted it will.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions," City said in a statement.

"The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums."

To make its appeal, City would need to send an email to the chair of the independent commission's three-person panel, who would then appoint a new appeal board — also consisting of three people, one of whom "shall have held judicial office", according to the Premier League handbook.

The board will then schedule a hearing that should finish within 12 weeks after the appeal is filed and not exceed five consecutive days.

Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) and chief executive Ferran Soriano in 2024. (AP: Dave Thompson)

Sanctions will be decided later

City's punishment will be addressed in a separate, confidential hearing with the independent commission.

The Premier League statement didn't mention whether sanctions could be imposed before the decision of the appeal was reached, only that it was the league's intention that the process be concluded "as soon as possible".

According to the Premier League, the independent commission could issue a reprimand, fine, suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expel the club from the competition.

Clubs have been expelled from lower leagues in England but never from the Premier League.

A club that is expelled from the Premier League could apply for membership in the English Football League, which runs the three divisions below the Premier League: the Championship, League One and League Two. The EFL's regulations say it "could be asked to accommodate any former Premier League Club(s) in League Two".

The biggest points deduction handed to a Premier League team was 10 to Everton in 2023, for overspending in one three-year financial period. That deduction was later reduced to six after an appeal.

City's breaches are much more widespread and included a refusal to cooperate, unlike Everton.

Some have called for criminal charges

The Man City case is a disciplinary proceeding, not a criminal investigation. However, some have suggested that British authorities also should look at the matter.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled, then it is potentially a criminal matter," Lord Cruddas, a Conservative peer, told the BBC.

"The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

According to the Fraud Act of 2006, individuals can face up to 10 years in prison if they are found to have dishonestly made a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss.

There have been no reports of any criminal investigation in the case.

City sponsor Etihad Airways considers legal action

Etihad Airways, City's main sponsor, was considering legal against the Premier League for the way the investigation findings were communicated, Sky News reported late on Wednesday.

Sky News quoted an Etihad statement saying "we stand with the club", adding that the Abu Dhabi-based airline said it would "seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests … at no time did the Premier League reach out to or engage with Etihad in the process associated with the commission's opinion".

Rival teams could make claims for compensation

No club has publicly announced its intention to make a compensation claim based on the impact of City's rule-breaking. However, the BBC has reported that a number of clubs had started seeking advice over whether they would have a case for financial compensation, before the verdict had been announced.

A precedent was set this year when Everton was ordered to pay more than 35 million pounds ($67 million) in compensation to Burnley, which successfully argued to a disciplinary commission that it would have survived relegation — at Everton's expense — in the 2021–22 campaign had its rival been given its six-point penalty for the financial breaches that season.

In City's case, top teams could argue they lost out on titles or Champions League qualification — worth tens of millions of dollars each season — because of City's conduct, and weaker teams could claim defeats to City's expensively assembled squads contributed to relegation or lower finishing positions in the league standings, and therefore reduced prize money.

AP

title: How a breast cancer trial changed the lives of survivors
text:
Donna Rullo wasn't going down without a fight.

It was early 2001, and then-40-year-old Ms Rullo had just been diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer.

Up to one in five cases of breast cancer are HER2-positive, which means the cancer cells have higher than normal levels of human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2) protein, promoting growth of the cancer itself.

It's an aggressive and fast-growing cancer, but typically responds well to targeted treatments.

When Ms Rullo was diagnosed, targeted treatments weren't an option in Australia.

But 25 years ago, she took a leap of faith and joined a drug trial that changed the course of her life, and that of countless women after her.

More than two decades after having it cut off, Donna Rullo still has her hair in this same gold box. (Supplied: Donna Rullo)

When Ms Rullo heard about now-retired oncologist Richard Bell's involvement with a trial for a new drug called trastuzumab, she drove five hours from her regional fruit farm to Melbourne for one of his lectures.

Ms Rullo says she rang him once a week before securing a position on the HERA (HERceptin Adjuvant) trial, which went on to enrol more than 5,000 patients from 39 countries.

How to enrol in a clinical trial In his open letter to all Australians, the late Richard Scolyer wrote of the pride he felt taking part in clinical trials.

She recalls being motivated to watch her son, now 37, grow up.

"I went through 10 years of IVF to have him, my son's 12 and he needs me and I want to be here," she says.

She still remembers getting the call.

"He said: 'It's Richard, I just wanted to tell you, you're patient number one of the HERA trial,'" she says.

"I just cried and cried. I couldn't stop. I was so emotional."

The trial went on to show that taking the drug trastuzumab for a year "significantly improves long-term disease-free survival" for patients with HER2-positive early breast cancer.

"It was the first drug that really showed promise and women were just thinking: 'Oh my God, finally we have something we can all hold onto,'" Ms Rullo says.

Donna Rullo had chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy before joining the trastuzumab trial. (Supplied: Donna Rullo)

The drug with a $50K price tag

Twenty years ago today, trastuzumab was added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) for the treatment of patients with HER-2 positive early-stage breast cancer.

It's a move which Breast Cancer Network Australia founder and then-chief executive Lyn Swinburne says has been "life-changing" for thousands of Australian women since.

Trastuzumab is now the most common HER2-targeted therapy offered to patients in Australia and New Zealand.

It may be given alongside surgery, chemotherapy, radiation or other HER2-targeted treatments, and works by attaching itself to the cancer cell HER2 receptor.

Lyn Swinburne was diagnosed with breast cancer in 1993. (Supplied: Lyn Swinburne)

Before its inclusion on the PBS, women not on trials like Ms Rullo were paying between $50,000 and $70,000 a year for treatment, or went without.

It was an accessibility gap that Ms Swinburne and then-Breast Cancer Network Australia board member, breast cancer survivor and former Olympian Raelene Boyle wanted to address.

"I was hearing from women who were selling their houses, selling their holiday houses, selling their farms to try and get this drug," Ms Swinburne says.

"Probably knowing it wasn't going to save their lives necessarily, but it was going to extend their lives, and especially when you've got young children, that's really, really important."

In June 2001, they invited prime minister John Howard to Ms Boyle's 50th birthday, sitting him between them as they lobbied for the drug to be subsidised.

"We basically talked to him all night about this drug and the difference it made," Ms Boyle recalls.

Raelene Boyle, pictured with former prime minister John Howard, described her 50th as a great party. (Supplied: BCNA)

In late 2001, the government announced a special program which allowed women with HER-2 positive metastatic breast cancer to access the drug for free.

Then, on October 1, 2006, it was added to the PBS for the treatment of patients with HER-2 positive early-stage breast cancer.

Breast cancer outcomes improving

Breast cancer is very common in Australia, with one in seven women diagnosed with the disease over their lifetime.

Although more people in Australia are being diagnosed with breast cancer each year, Breast Cancer Network Australia chief executive Kirsten Pilatti says survivors are also living longer than ever before.

"Survival has certainly improved because we know more about the specifics of different breast cancers," she says.

In 2017–2021, the chance of surviving at least five years post-diagnosis was 93 per cent, up from 75 per cent in 1987–1991.

Rachel Dear, a medical oncologist at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney, says improved survival rates have been driven by earlier detection and diagnosis, improved awareness and "more personalised and targeted" treatments.

Rachel Dear says personalised treatment options for patients have led to improved outcomes. (Supplied: Rachel Dear)

Understanding more about how different types of cancer behave and respond to treatment allows specialists to tailor treatments to each patient, Dr Dear says.

"Treatment has changed depending on which subtype of breast cancer we're looking at," she says.

"There are three main types of breast cancer, and within each of those three types, there are more drug treatment options that have improved survival rates.

"In 2026, we have a number of new drug treatments to offer patients."

'Taboo' cancer side effects we don't talk about Shame and stigma mean gynaecological side-effects from cancer treatment — affecting women's sexual, urinary and reproductive health — are under-reported and under-researched.

Breast cancer's huge public profile means there is greater awareness of the disease, Dr Dear says, but has also led to greater investment in research and clinical trials, resulting in more treatment options for patients.

Ms Rullo considers herself lucky to have seen her son grow into a "remarkable" man, marry and have two kids of his own.

She encourages people facing an uncertain health diagnosis to learn as much as they can and to advocate for themselves, if needed.

"Life could have completely gone a different way, who knows what could have happened if I didn't fight to be on that trial," she says.

title: Putting off your tax return? You have a month to file
text:
A big tax deadline is looming, with the start of October kicking the countdown into gear.

Here's what you need to know if you haven't filed your tax return for the 2025–26 financial year yet.

When are tax returns due?

The due date this year is Monday, November 2.

Usually, people who do their own tax returns must lodge them by October 31.

But this year, that falls on a Saturday.

And the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) says that if October 31 falls on a weekend, the due date is the next business day.

So, this year, the due date is actually on Monday, November 2.

If you're having a tax agent file your return, they'll generally have a special lodgement schedule, which means they may be able to lodge returns for clients later than November 2.

However, the ATO says you need to engage a tax agent before October 31 if you're going down this path, so make sure you book your appointment before the end of the month.

You can file your tax return via the ATO's online portal. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

Is there a fine for filing late?

There can be.

But the ATO says it considers a person's individual circumstances before deciding what action to take and whether they'll be sent a failure to lodge (FTL) notice.

"We recognise that sometimes people don't meet their lodgement obligations on time, even with the best intentions," the ATO says.

"Generally, we don't apply penalties in isolated cases of late lodgement."

You can expect to hear from the ATO before getting a penalty notice.

"If you fail to lodge on time, we'll warn you by phone or in writing before we apply a failure to lodge penalty and issue you a notice to lodge," the ATO says.

"This will give you the opportunity to lodge or give you the opportunity to engage with us if you're experiencing circumstances preventing you from lodging."

Will I get a tax refund?

"Some workers genuinely are owed a refund due to over-withholding or legitimate deductions," said Jenny Wong, the tax lead at accounting body CPA Australia.

"But a significant group overestimates what they'll receive."

Don't expect a post-budget $1,250 boost this tax time The $1,000 instant tax reduction and the $250 Working Australians Tax Offset won't be in play at tax time this year.

Part of the expectation for a tax refund comes from the days of the low and middle income tax offset (LMITO).

For Australians earning up to $126,000, LMITO delivered a tax break ranging from $255 to $1,080 in 2018–19, 2019–20 and 2020–21.

There was a one-off increase to ease cost-of-living pressures in 2021–22, lifting the base amount to $675 and the full amount to $1,500.

"LMITO created an expectation of a tax refund in prior years," Ms Wong said.

And even though that offset ended years ago, its impact on the Australian mindset about tax returns has lingered.

The LMITO hangover

The hangover from the LMITO years may have led some to assume this year's budget announcements would result in a $1,250 cash payment in their tax returns, when that's not the case.

But it's more than that.

Our tax returns can have complications we didn't anticipate (more on that below), and we may have overestimated how much deductions will benefit us.

For example, it's easy to assume a few thousand dollars in work expenses and charity donations will all come back to us as a refund.

But the way deductions are calculated often means taxpayers receive only a small fraction of that money back.

"Australia has a clear culture around deductions," said Elizabeth Morton, a senior lecturer at Curtin University and chartered accountant.

"A lot of errors taxpayers make relate to problems with deductions."

Dr Morton said that included:

claiming things that aren't deductible

not being able to substantiate an expense

not apportioning how much of their deduction is used outside of work

not claiming in line with prescribed methods

claiming capital expenditure outright

"All of these will likely result in over-claiming of deductions, therefore underpayment of tax," Dr Morton said.

People can run into complications in their tax returns they didn't anticipate. (ABC News: Lindsay Dunbar)

How much should we be getting back?

Obviously there's no one answer to this question. It really depends on your own personal circumstances.

However, let's assume you have only one job and no income from other sources, no work-related deductions, and no donations to charities in the past financial year.

"If the employer calculates Pay As You Go salary withholding tax correctly, it should generally cover an employee's final tax bill," Ms Wong said.

"The employee should not expect a tax refund."

It's a good idea to approach filing your tax return with low expectations.

"We need to be careful of assuming that we will get a refund each year," Dr Morton said.

But aren't we entitled to claim?

There's a balance to strike here, because there are plenty of legitimate reasons to claim deductions on your tax return.

And Dr Morton said the onus was on taxpayers to get it right.

"It is important that taxpayers understand that they are permitted by law to claim deductions that are allowable," she said.

"So taxpayers can miss out on deductions if they are not aware of the rules, or if they don't keep proper records."

Think writing off something on tax makes it free? It doesn't Advertisers tout EOFY sales as a prime time for big buys, and hint at the promise of a generous tax refund, but that's not quite how it works.

The taxation system can seem daunting, so many people turn to accountants to help them navigate the process.

While the cost of using professionals to prepare your tax return is tax deductible, the up-front cost for an accountant can be prohibitive.

There are, however, a series of free tax clinics around the country that offer eligible people help to file their tax returns.

Many of those clinics are in major cities, but some do offer virtual sessions for people in regional and rural areas.

You can check if you're eligible for free tax assistance here and check out the nearest tax clinic to you here.

The ATO also has a comprehensive guide to deductions according to a range of industries.

So why is my tax return so low this year?

"There could be multiple reasons why people are caught off guard by minimal refunds or tax bills," Ms Wong said.

"A worker working multiple jobs but then ticks the box on their Tax File Number (TFN) declaration form telling all their employers to stop taxing the first $18,200 from their pay — meaning each employer withholds less tax than they should.

"Or the worker may have student HELP/HECS debts but did not tick the box to withhold extra from their pay."

The Medicare levy surcharge may also catch higher earners out if they don't have what the Australian Taxation Office defines as appropriate private health insurance.

"Whether they have private health insurance can lead to some issues, particularly if their income is above the threshold, or the rebate rate they are claiming is not aligned to their income," Dr Morton said.

The threshold for paying the Medicare levy surcharge is more than $101,000 for singles and $202,000 (plus $1,500 for each dependent child after the first one) for families.

title: Businesses fear visa changes to backpacker visas will make staffing harder
text:
Businesses across Western Australia's north are worried recent visa changes will mean fewer backpackers choose to work in remote regions where they are most needed.

The federal government has recently announced changes to the Working Holiday Maker visa program, which could influence decisions of backpackers coming to Australia in the future.

"I did come here to work towards my third year visa, and if that wasn't an option, I would never have come here," Zac Cederholm said.

The American barista moved to Kununurra, about 3,000 kilometres north of Perth, a few years ago and now manages a cafe — but said he would not have ventured this remote today.

Zac Cederholm says working holiday visa extensions play a key role in attracting and retaining visitors to remote Australia. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Fewer incentives, fewer workers

Backpackers wanting to extend their visas for a second or third year must work in regional or remote Australia — 88 days for a second year, and six months for a third.

Under the government's changes, which are being progressively rolled out over the next year, Immigration Minister Tony Burke said backpackers would also have to enter a ballot, with third-year extensions capped at 5,000, down from 31,000 this year.

Mr Cederholm said these changes would make it less attractive for backpackers to come to remote Australia, where they currently do essential jobs like picking fruit, stacking shelves and serving tables.

Many businesses in the Kimberley are staffed by backpackers. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"If you can have staff that stay around for potentially six months, that's consistency, that's reliability," he said.

Mr Cederholm said the visa changes would also do very little to ease some of the region's ongoing issues like housing, with most temporary migrants in the Kimberley living in hostels, dongas and share houses.

"I don't know any backpackers that have taken up single houses," he said.

" If we had to rely solely on local staffing, I think there'd be a lot less businesses in town. "

Frustration and uncertainty

Australia's North West Tourism chief executive Bill Tatchell said he was calling for common sense in relation to "essential" backpackers.

Bill Tatchell says visa changes affecting backpackers are "devastating" for the region. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

He said the policy was "incredibly frustrating" and would reduce the incentive for backpackers to undertake regional jobs.

"Fundamentally, there's an economic loss and it's just beggars belief a decision can be made that can have such an impact in regions," Mr Tatchell said.

The federal government has previously pointed to guest workers from the Pacific, brought to Australia under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme, as a potential source of workers impacted by the backpacker restrictions.

But East Kimberley Chamber of Commerce chief executive Keda Bond said businesses were "definitely nervous" about the future.

She said the reduction in third-year visas would be "devastating" for the region, which relied on seasonal workers.

Keda Bond says a reduction in backpacker numbers was bad news for business in remote Australia. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"If five businesses close in one of our towns, like Kununurra, for example, that is felt by the whole town, the whole region, and there is an actual reduction in services," Ms Bond said.

"I feel the government is making changes without considering regional Australia at all."

She described the reform as a "kick in the gut" for remote businesses, already struggling after the changes to visa processing priorities to curb net overseas migration.

Haydn Sale is general manager of Yougawalla Pastoral Company, which is reopening a major abattoir near Broome.

The long-awaited opening of Pindan Beef Co has been delayed until next year. (Supplied: Haydn Sale)

But the abattoir Pindan Beef Company, struggled with skilled workers, with only one application from an Australian resident and a number of skilled workers whose visas were "held up in the system", according to Mr Sale.

Mr Sale travelled to Canberra to lobby politicians to fast-track the visa applications and help secure the workers needed for the abattoir to reopen.

"I was pleasantly surprised that you can get into Parliament House and you can rattle around and make your case," Mr Sale said.

But he believes if he did not travel to Canberra, his case may never have been heard.

title: RBA relaxed about housing downturn, deeply worried by AI and bonds
text:
Despite Australia's rapid housing downturn, which threatens to be the worst in decades, the Reserve Bank believes the main threats to the nation's financial stability come from overseas.

That is the key takeaway from its latest half-yearly Financial Stability Review (FSR), released two days after the bank increased its cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent on Tuesday.

While Australian households remain among the world's most indebted, a rise in real household disposable income per capita since a recent low point in 2023 and 2024 means most borrowers are better placed to cope with their mortgage repayments, even though rates have passed the peak of 4.35 per cent in that period.

As at the end of June, the RBA estimated that less than 2 per cent of variable-rate owner-occupier mortgage borrowers had a "cash flow shortfall" — that is, where their income was insufficient to cover scheduled mortgage repayments and essential expenses.

The RBA forecast that this might rise to 2 per cent, or slightly above, in coming months as the cash rate has risen once since then to 4.6 per cent and is expected by financial markets to potentially rise further.

'Pressures bearing down' on rates Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?

However, this is well below peaks close to 5 per cent in 2023 and 2024 during the post-COVID inflation spike, when the cash rate rose rapidly to 4.35 per cent.

The bank also noted that the median, or middle of the range, borrower has offset and/or redraw buffers that would cover more than a year of scheduled mortgage repayments at current interest rates.

Even if borrowers find themselves unable to make their mortgage repayments, the bank said most would be able to sell their home in order to pay off their loan in full.

It estimated that less than 1 per cent of borrowers were in negative equity and owing more on their loan than the market value of their home.

The RBA noted that even a 20 per cent plunge in house prices would only see around 5 per cent of mortgages falling into negative equity, due to the substantial run-up in property values ahead of the latest downturn.

Australia faces 'biggest property downturn in 40 years' Australian house prices have fallen for a sixth month in a row, with falls of up to 15 per cent forecast.

The central bank also modelled a "very adverse downturn", where unemployment increases to 6.3 per cent (from 4.6 per cent currently), inflation nearly doubles to 7 per cent and the cash rate climbs a further percentage point to 5.6 per cent.

Even under this scenario, it estimated that just 5 per cent of mortgage borrowers would be "at a higher risk of defaulting on their loans", similar to levels seen in 2023.

Global threats 'continue to mount', Australia 'unlikely to be immune'

While the Reserve Bank is relatively relaxed about the domestic situation, it warned ominously that "threats to international financial stability continue to mount".

It cautioned that the interaction of intractable global conflicts disrupting key supply chains, the pace of technological development and the disruptions it causes, and the increase of severe weather events due to climate change, are key threats which "could be making a system-wide shock more likely and its potential consequences more severe".

Loading...

Reflecting recent comments from the RBA governor and other senior officials, the bank warned that a bursting of the potential AI bubble could trigger broader financial fallout.

"Low risk premia in major equity and credit markets have contributed to buoyant financial conditions for businesses, but these risk premia could move sharply higher in response to an adverse shock potentially in a disorderly manner," the review noted.

" One possible trigger could be a shift in sentiment towards the AI investment boom, which is increasingly fuelled by expectations of sustained rapid earnings growth and a debt-financing cycle that is becoming more opaque and circular. "

While the RBA noted that hyperscalers and hardware producers were generally viewed as lower risk due to alternative revenue streams and generally solid financial positions, there are "pockets of higher risk firms in the AI value chain", including data centre construction, utility and neocloud providers.

It also noted the rising risks even for the large hyperscalers and hardware producers at the centre of the AI boom.

Interest rate hike could be short-lived The Reserve Bank will increase interest rates on Tuesday, but three factors outside the bank's control are pulling rates in different directions.

"The AI industry has been increasingly using off-balance sheet arrangements to finance large projects, such as data centres," the FSR observed.

These "opaque" arrangements sit outside of the hyperscalers' balance sheets for now, but the RBA warned "their financial obligations to these projects are becoming significant, with estimates ranging from $US1 trillion to $US1.5 trillion", or $1.4 trillion to $2 trillion.

The RBA also highlighted concerns about "circular financing" within the AI sector, for example where chipmakers provided financial support to neocloud firms who then purchased their products.

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

While there are financial risks posed by a collapse of the AI boom, the RBA also noted increasing risks if that boom continued.

A key concern is increasing vulnerabilities to AI-driven cyber attacks, especially the reliance of financial institutions on a small number of critical technology service providers.

In addition, it warned of financial market risks around "herd behaviour and market correlation" as AI agents played a greater role in investment decisions.

Loading

RBA concerned about risks of 'disruptive sell-off' in bond market

Another key global risk that is concerning the Reserve Bank is the recent jump in key advanced economy government bond yields, including the increased participation of investors, such as hedge funds, loading up on debt to play the market.

Why rates are headed higher for longer Against the backdrop of war in Iran, a trade war with Canada and bond sell-offs, trust in the US dollar appears to be weakening, and it will likely have an impact when the RBA announces its rate decision today.

The RBA noted that hedge fund "repo" debt was near record highs, at more than $US3 trillion for US hedge funds alone, which was equivalent to about 10 per cent of that nation's annual GDP.

"This raises the prospect of increased volatility — and potentially a disruptive sell-off — in core bond markets that are central to the operation of the global financial system," the bank warned in the FSR.

title: Buzzard iron ore mine dispute leaves workers in limbo
text:
About 200 jobs at an iron ore mine in South Australia's far north are in limbo amid a financial dispute between the project's owner and a major onsite contractor, the ABC understands.

In a letter to staff seen by ABC News, contractor Agile Mining Services said work would be shut down at the Buzzard mine site south of Coober Pedy.

The project is owned by Central Iron — a subsidiary of Peak Iron, whose website states the Buzzard mine extracts high-grade hematite for shipment.

In the letter, Agile told workers to use leave if available and to expect further advice once a "commercial position" had been resolved.

"Agile is therefore shutting down site operations and directing its own personnel to cease normal duties, with employees to utilise available annual leave … where applicable," it stated.

ABC News has contacted Peak Iron for comment, but is yet to receive a response.

The situation comes amid uncertainty about steelmaking in SA, following the revelation that more than 600 jobs will go at the Whyalla steelworks and associated industries.

The site is south of Coober Pedy. (Google Maps)

But Mining Minister Tom Koutsantonis said the situation at the Buzzard site was an "internal dispute" that did not reflect on the mine itself.

"This is not about them not being a viable mine or there not being the work — this is a dispute about cost," he said.

"This is a question of a mining company who's hired a contractor to do the mining, and they're having a dispute about how much they're paying the contractor to do the mining."

He said the government was not party to the dispute and would not be intervening, but suspected there would be a quick resolution.

"The contractor has stood down and is now negotiating with the mining company about the cost of the mining," he said.

"I'm pretty sure they'll sort that out relatively quickly and they'll get back to mining."

title: How a five-hour Woollahra Council meeting quickly turned personal
text:

NationalNSWCity life How a five-hour Woollahra Council meeting quickly turned personal Cindy Yin October 1, 2026 — 3:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A fiery five-hour council meeting took a personal turn when the Woollahra mayor revealed she looked up the value of a pro-housing advocate’s home during a debate over plans to add 9400 homes to Sydney’s eastern suburbs. There was only one item on the agenda at Woollahra Council’s extraordinary meeting on Wednesday night – to finalise how the council would respond to the most significant rezoning of the eastern suburbs in decades. Under state government plans unveiled last month, housing density would be concentrated around Woollahra and Edgecliff train stations, building towers up to 32 and 34 storeys. One admission tipped the temperature inside Woollahra Council’s chambers almost to boiling point. Wolter Peeters More than 10 pro-housing advocates spoke at the public forum and were met with staunch opposition and questioning from some of the 13 councillors who attended. The meeting featured numerous interjections and tetchy back-and-forth exchanges, and multiple points of order were called. At one point, Liberal mayor Sarah Dixson said she was “one word away” from calling an adjournment to turn the temperature down. About 40 minutes into the five-hour-long meeting, it was a personal question that almost tipped the temperature in the room to boiling point.

Advertisement

It began when councillor Mary-Lou Jarvis asked Sydney YIMBY’s chair Justin Simon if he could afford to buy a freestanding house with a median price of $5.4 million in Elizabeth Bay, quoting figures from realestate.com.au. “I could not afford to buy a house in Woollahra [council area] anywhere,” Simon responded. Loading Dixson interjected and revealed she had looked up Simon’s home address before he spoke at the meeting: “Hang on, I mean, I’ve looked at the cost of your house, and you certainly could afford to, you certainly could. “The cost of his home, according to realestate.com, is more than the average price in Woollahra.”

Advertisement

Simon’s reaction was one of disbelief: “Sorry, so the cost of my home ... So you’ve taken my address that I signed up for to speak at council, and you’ve then gone and looked up my home on realestate.com? That’s such a bizarre … ” “Yes, because realestate.com is such a reliable source of information,” Dixson quipped. Before their terse exchange drew to a close, Simon called on the mayor to share where she lived or how much her house was worth, to which she responded curtly: “I don’t own a house.” Simon has since criticised Dixson for accessing his private address through a form he submitted to the council, and said it was a “gotcha moment” aimed at “launching personal attacks on speakers” if they did not agree with her views on the state government’s housing plan. “I’ve spoken at councils dozens of times over the last few years, and I’ve never had anything like this happen before,” he said. “How can people have confidence signing up to speak at Woollahra Council knowing that this is how their information is handled? This kind of privacy violation will have a chilling effect on community participation.”

Advertisement

Related Article Planning ‘It’s like a village’: What Woollahra residents really think about 10,000 new homes To register to speak at public forums, members of the public fill out a form and provide their full name, address, phone number and email address. Speakers must agree to a condition that states their face, voice and personal information will be recorded and publicly accessible on the council’s website. Asked why she accessed Simon’s address, Dixson said: “It’s publicly available information and was relevant to proving that claims made by the speaker were simply incorrect. “The vast majority of people who attended the meeting were there for all the right reasons.”

Advertisement

Dixson did not respond when asked if she had breached the code of conduct or searched for the addresses of any other speakers, and she did not confirm if she accessed Simon’s details independently or through a council staff member. Simon said the mayor’s action strayed far from debate about public policy and was an attempt to turn the conversation personal. “It potentially is a way to discourage participation from your opponents,” he said. “It reflects the weakness of her position that she feels the need to fall back on that.” Simon said he would submit a complaint to the Office of Local Government. Under Woollahra Council’s code of conduct policy, which sets the minimum standards of behaviour, integrity and performance expected, councillors must “only access council information needed for council business, and not use that council information for private purposes”. Academic Andy Asquith, who researches governance matters in local councils, said the behaviour benchmarks had vague wording and therefore made it unclear whether the mayor had breached the policy.

Advertisement

“It’s not a level playing field – you expect everyone is playing by the same rules … That sort of information is operational and should be accessed by a very small number of council employees, so the fact that the mayor accessed it is where the issue lies,” Asquith said. title: Nine Australians die of breast cancer every day. So why do we underestimate the disease?
text:
