LifestyleHealth & wellnessBreast cancer Nine Australians die of breast cancer every day. So why do we underestimate the disease? Shona Hendley Updated October 1, 2026 — 3:07pm ,first published 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before 33-year-old Chontaine Adair was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic breast cancer in 2025, she had a very different perception of the disease. “I just didn’t think it could happen at my age, and I had a mindset that it couldn’t happen to me,” says Adair, who is based in Sydney. Chontaine and Landis Adair with their daughters Paisley, 7, and Xanthie, 6. Wolter Peeters This misconception, says the mother of two, was partly shaped by age-specific cancer-screening advice. “I didn’t know anyone in their early thirties with breast cancer, and any ads regarding checks like mammograms, for example, show older women and even mention, ‘If you are [a certain] age, get tested’, and this age was always older. They were not directed to younger women,” Adair explains. A new survey, funded by the National Breast Cancer Foundation (NBCF) as part of their Breast Cancer Awareness Month campaign, Unfinished Stories, has revealed that, as in Adair’s case, there is a disconnect between public perception and the reality of breast cancer today.

Advertisement

The survey, completed by 1003 respondents, found that 64 per cent underestimated the number of people diagnosed each year, 84 per cent underestimated the likelihood of recurrence and spread, and 51 per cent underestimated the number of Australians who die from breast cancer each day. Related Article Lunch with A little over half of women accept a free mammogram. Cassandra’s rare form of breast cancer wouldn’t have been detected without it Additionally, it found that nearly two-thirds (64 per cent) now see breast cancer as more manageable than other cancers, and over half (53 per cent) believe treatment advances have fundamentally altered public perceptions of the disease. Dr Cleola Anderiesz, chief executive of the NBCF, believes these findings reflect progress achieved through decades of research, including reducing Australia’s breast cancer death rate by more than 40 per cent over the past three decades, but also highlight a perception gap. “Research has transformed breast cancer outcomes. Yet breast cancer remains one of our most significant health challenges,” she says.

Advertisement

“The biggest gaps we’re seeing are around the scale and ongoing impact of breast cancer. Many people underestimate how many people are diagnosed each year [approximately 20,000], how likely breast cancer is to return or spread, and how many lives are still lost to the disease every day [approximately nine].” Specialist breast cancer surgeon Dr Chantel Thornton, who was not involved in the research, says that from her experience and among her patient cohort – predominantly premenopausal women – it’s very uncommon for them not to take the diagnosis seriously, but that some do underestimate the disease. Underestimating the seriousness of breast cancer can lead to decreased urgency around breast changes, say experts. iStock “Patients may underestimate the fact that breast cancer can metastasise to other organs, and therefore it is harder to treat them for a cure,” she says. Additionally, Thornton says some “people don’t understand that all breast cancers are not the same and different subtypes can infer different survival”.

Advertisement

A lack of understanding, or incorrect perception, can pose a range of risks at the individual level. “When people underestimate the seriousness of breast cancer, they may also underestimate the importance of breast awareness, screening and seeking medical advice about breast changes,” says Anderiesz. Loading It can also have a much broader effect, particularly in supporting ongoing research into the disease. Breast cancer still remains the second leading cause of cancer death in Australian women, says Professor Belinda Parker, NBCF-funded researcher at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre.

Advertisement

“Breast cancer is not just one disease; it changes. Everyone has their own individual cancer, and so some people have a type of cancer that has a very poor survival rate, and we can’t forget about those women.” Related Article Breast cancer The common breast cancer myth that might be putting women at risk Parker says continued investment in research is critical to build on the progress made and to investigate other areas of breast cancer that haven’t received as much attention. “We haven’t really made a big dent in women who get metastatic cancer, so when their cancer has spread to other sites … we also haven’t really made a big difference for treating diseases that have spread to the bone,” she says. “What we really need to do is focus on either preventing the deadly types of breast cancer or being able to target them head-on, and that’s where research is critical.”

Advertisement

Now, nearly a year after Adair’s diagnosis, following radiation and ongoing hormone-targeted treatment, her mindset and perception of breast cancer have changed. “I know now that it can happen to anyone at any age, and I now know breast cancer looks different for everyone, and that different types require different treatments.” Another key takeaway for Adair is that she now recognises the benefits of cancer research firsthand. “My targeted therapy is the result of research, and hopefully more treatment options will be developed by research in the future to help me give me time to watch my girls grow up, and others live long, healthier lives.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. title: ‘I would be very concerned’: Trainer prays rain stays away for unbeaten Kiwi’s Epsom challenge

Cambridge trainer Stephen Marsh concedes New Zealand form has been “a bit sketchy” in recent times. And he believes his unbeaten mare Well Written could have been treated better at the weights for her shot at the $1.5 million group 1 Epsom Handicap (1600m) on Saturday at Randwick, when she races outside New Zealand for the first time. Unbeaten New Zealand mare Well Written with trainer Stephen Marsh at Randwick. Jessica Hromas But he is also confident he has “the right horse for the job” – if the heavy rain stays away. Well Written, a two-time group 1 winner, is set to make her much-anticipated debut in Australia before taking on star Victorian mare Sheza Alibi in the $10 million Golden Eagle at Randwick on October 31.

The four-year-old arrived on Tuesday night and is staying at the former Leilani Lodge stables at Randwick now leased by Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott. A $32,500 weanling and $80,000 yearling buy before powerhouse Yulong acquired a 50 per cent share a year ago, Well Written took all before her as a three-year-old, winning six times, including a photo-finish victory over subsequent group 1 Vinery Stud Stakes champion Belle Cheval in the $4 million Kiwi (1500m). Well Written could start favourite in front of Autumn Boy (pictured) in Saturday’s Epsom at Randwick. Getty Images The daughter of Written Tycoon returned with a dominant victory in the group 1 weight-for-age Proisir Plate (1400m) four weeks ago at Ellerslie and Marsh said “she looks exceptionally good”. After drawing well in barrier three, Marsh’s main concern is the possibility of a rain-affected track. The forecast is for a high chance of showers late on Friday and into Saturday, when there is also the potential for thunderstorms. She has never raced on heavy going.

“It’s one of the great handicaps, and it’s exciting to bring an unbeaten horse over,” said Marsh, whose biggest win this side of the Tasman was with Sofia Rose in the 2016 group 1 Australian Oaks. “We certainly didn’t get the visitors’ draw, and hopefully the weather is good. “Early on, she trialled up on a wet track and couldn’t really go on that; she ran about fourth or fifth. We call her a New Zealander, but she’s by Written Tycoon, so she’s sort of half New Zealand. But she doesn’t ultimately like wet tracks, so if a storm does come, I would be very concerned.” Well Written, backed into $3.50 favouritism on Thursday over a drifting Autumn Boy ($4), was given 55 kilograms for the Epsom, a weight that surprised Marsh. “I’m certainly not one to complain or anything like that, but I didn’t quite probably expect 55,” he said of his first Epsom runner.

“Probably a couple of horses in the race I didn’t expect us to be so close to, so it’s certainly not going to be an easy job with 55, but that’s the way it’s been handicapped. “I was very surprised when we got half a kilo less than Autumn Boy and where the ratings are, but that’s the way they do it. I thought it’s quite an even line-up and some of those horses are maybe a touch out of form, but then they probably get into an Epsom quite well.” He expects “the most exciting galloper” he has trained to handle the trip well and show she is the finished product.

title: An office chat about ‘Wharfie Time’ upset a colleague. What went wrong?
text:

BusinessWorkplaceAsk an expert Opinion An office chat about ‘Wharfie Time’ upset a colleague. What went wrong? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor October 1, 2026 — 3:00pm

October 1, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I returned to work after the long weekend in Melbourne and the office was buzzing with chatter about the AFL Grand Final. I am not a footy fan, so usually don’t really participate in such discussions, but I had been invited to a grand final party and watched the game this year. I have to admit it was very exciting. Unfortunately, I seem to have made a bad mistake on the Monday after. I innocently asked what “Wharfie Time” was, something I hadn’t got a grasp of on the day. A colleague replied with words along the lines of: “It was a disaster – that’s what it was”. Then another colleague who wasn’t part of the conversation, but was within earshot, became very upset. We haven’t seen them since. What did I accidentally bring about? A colleague who wasn’t part of the conversation, but was within earshot, became very upset. John Shakespeare The person who became upset and fled the scene was unquestionably a Fremantle supporter. The Fremantle Dockers are the AFL’s second Western Australian team. They joined the league in 1995. Unlike their larger cousins, the West Coast Eagles, who joined in 1987 and had won the premiership (finished the champions of the entire competition) within six years, the Dockers have never reached that pinnacle. Saturday’s game was their best chance to break their drought. They had finished on top of the ladder at the end of the home and away season (the part of the football calendar that precedes finals) and at times looked invincible.

Advertisement

The grand final was a brilliant, close-fought game, but with less than five minutes to go in the last quarter, it looked like Fremantle had repeated a pattern that had defined their season: they had weathered the best football their opponent could muster and had accelerated towards victory. In short: never underestimate the power of football to affect people’s emotions. This is where Wharfie Time comes in. What you saw on the telecast was a kind of in-game celebration (I’ve seen it referred to as an “activation”, a term that makes me want to gag). I’d call it a crowd provocation in the form of a strange assortment of in-jokes and homages. Until the grand final, it had only happened twice before. Only this season. And only at Fremantle’s home ground in Perth. Fremantle sought permission from the AFL to use it at the grand final (under the right circumstances), and the AFL reportedly encouraged it. “Wharfie” is the Australian term for a dockworker, a name originally considered by the club administrators as the football club’s nickname, but sidestepped due to perceived political connotations. In 2009, however, the Dockers’ captain, Matthew Pavlich, addressed the playing group before a match while wearing a mic and implored his team to “Put on your superman capes, boys! It’s wharfie time!” (They lost the game comfortably.)

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Job hunting Why your closest friends probably won’t help you find a job Tim Duggan Work columnist The whole thing starts with a baleful funeral toll, taken directly from the AC/DC song Hells Bells. In Perth, the lights go out at this point, and it’s here that the similarity to the entrance of The Undertaker in WWE wrestling is impossible to ignore. In this way, it’s not just “sports entertainment,” it’s a pastiche of sports entertainment. A reference on top of a reference on top of a reference. While DNG! DNG! DNG! echoes through the arena, the words “WHARFIE TIME” appear on the stadium screen and the crowd goes berserk. This all happened, with the exception of the lights, at the MCG on Saturday afternoon. A bit of fun? Maybe. Hindsight is a wonderful thing, but I would certainly say it was ill-advised in a grand final against a team notorious for never being beaten. In a game where the gods can be so capricious, never tempt fate. Immediately after this iteration of Wharfie Time, Brisbane commenced one of the greatest (and probably the fastest) comebacks in grand final history, kicking an almost unimaginably brilliant four goals in four minutes. After the game, numerous Brisbane players referred to the gimmick as a catalyst for their late surge.

Advertisement

So that’s the potted history. Let’s address the question of what you accidentally brought about? Football trauma, plain and simple. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Is it a good idea to mix business with pleasure? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor And this is the problem of office footy chat. It’s a great tradition – in Melbourne, certainly, and I’m sure throughout Australia. But for those not versed in the intricacies and earnestness of a certain kind of deep supporterdom (and for those who are, but have never truly fallen in love with a club), a stray word or off-hand comment on a Monday morning can cause great pain. This wasn’t your fault. It probably wasn’t even the fault of your blunt colleague – although surely if they knew there was a Dockers supporter nearby they could have been a touch more tactful. But it does highlight the fact that a thing undertaken in fun – whether that’s a water cooler chat about a weekend event or a premature celebration of a seemingly certain victory – can easily go sideways. In short: never underestimate the power of football to affect people’s emotions.

title: Augustus locks onto multiple gold zones near Leonora in WA
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Augustus locks onto multiple gold zones near Leonora in WA Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright October 1, 2026 — 2:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Augustus Minerals has defined at least two higher-grade gold shoots at its Music Well project in Western Australia’s prolific Leonora-Laverton gold district, with both remaining open along strike. The interpretation comes from a combination of recent diamond and reverse circulation (RC) drilling, assays and soil sampling. Augustus says its geological detective work has stitched together data from drilling and surface geochemistry to outline a western shoot defined by soil samples over 400 metres of strike and an eastern zone defined by pathfinder geochemistry over 300m. Both are open to the north-northeast at the company’s Clifton East prospect. Augustus Minerals’ reverse circulation drilling at its Music Well project in WA’s gold-rich Leonora-Laverton gold district. The interpretation links together a string of solid, earlier RC drill hits, including 11m at 2.41 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 32m, 8m at 3.27g/t gold from 72m and 34m at 0.83g/t gold from 38m. Pathfinder elements in soil samples, including tellurium, bismuth, molybdenum and tungsten, have helped trace the orientation of the mineralised structures.

Advertisement

‘Pathfinder geochemistry indicates a similar strike for the strong intersection seen in an RC drillhole within the eastern shoot.’ Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford A recent diamond drill hole put in by Augustus appears to have provided the final piece of the puzzle. While assays from the hole returned only lower-grade gold anomalism, including 6m at 0.31g/t gold from 79m, 5m at 0.43g/t gold from 106m and 12m at 0.22g/t gold from 117m, management believes the results are significant. According to Augustus, the core revealed tell-tale alteration from hematite to silica-sericite-pyrite-carbonate, which strengthened closer to the gold-bearing part of the system, suggesting the hole may have passed along the edge of a bigger mineralised zone. Crucially, structural measurements from the diamond core indicate that the higher-grade quartz-pyrite (iron sulphide) veins dip steeply to the southeast, providing a clear target for follow-up drilling. Armed with this new structural understanding, the company drilled a series of northwest-oriented RC holes to test for higher-density veining between the original drill holes. Assays from that program are pending and expected in mid to late October.

Advertisement

In addition to the two defined shoots, the company has its eye on a third target, a 200-metre-long zone of anomalous rock chip and soil pathfinder results. With rock chips grading up to 1.8g/t gold, the anomalism coincides with a major fault in the east of the Clifton East prospect. The company says this area has not yet been drill tested. Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford said: “Integration of surface geochemistry, RC and Diamond drilling data has outlined two higher-grade shoots within the broader alteration system that are open to the north-northeast.” The company’s Music Well project covers a commanding 1242 square kilometres of exploration tenure just 35km north of Leonora, a town that sits at the heart of a storied gold belt with a total endowment of more than 28 million ounces. Augustus’ ground abuts tenements held by regional giants Northern Star Resources and Genesis Minerals, with major gold projects in the neighbourhood including Darlot, King of the Hills and Thunderbox. The definition of coherent mineralised shoots comes at a time when the region is a hive of corporate activity. The Leonora–Laverton gold district is in the middle of a broader WA gold consolidation wave, with majors on the hunt for new ounces to feed their processing hubs. That backdrop helps explain why fresh exploration success in the area is attracting attention, with regional gold assets and land positions in the district increasingly in focus. Recent activity includes the eye-watering $12.6 billion Genesis-Vault merger in July and Brightstar Resources’ September acquisition of five critical exploration licences from Panther Metals immediately adjacent to its developing Laverton processing hub.

Advertisement

Of late, Genesis has been hoovering up gold ounces across Leonora and Laverton, building a formidable feed pipeline around its mills. It picked up Focus Minerals’ Laverton project to feed its restarted three-million-tonne-per-annum plant and splashed $639 million on Magnetic Resources to get exposure to the 2.24-million-ounce Lady Julie deposit in 2026. That buying spree followed a $600 million acquisition of St Barbara’s Leonora assets, including the Gwalia mine and mill, in 2023. With assays from its latest targeted RC drill campaign due shortly and drilling operations set to kick off once wet ground conditions improve, Augustus looks set to generate plenty of newsflow. In a part of the world where big miners are looking for their next meal, defining coherent, higher-grade gold shoots is one way for a junior to get a seat at the table. Erina Starkey October 1, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From today, patrons can now stand up with a drink outside pubs, restaurants and bars operating across the City of Sydney, scrapping a long-standing rule that prevented people drinking on the footpath without a table or shelf. The updated outdoor dining guideline are part of a wider push to make outdoor dining a permanent part of the city’s streets. This change affects all City of Sydney suburbs, from St Peters to Potts Point, Elizabeth Bay, Erskineville and the CBD. Removing the lingering hangover from the guidelines means punters can wait on the footpath with a glass of wine until their table is ready, and stand out the front of the pub drinking a beer, provided the venue has a designated outdoor dining area. The idea is that the change will add energy and life to public spaces, bringing Sydney closer to the outdoor dining and drinking culture of many European cities. Locals drink on the street outside the Forrester’s in Surry Hills. Matt Johnson, group beverage director at Applejack Group, which runs venues across the City of Sydney council area, including Opera Bar, Surry Hills’ Forrester’s and The Butler in Potts Point, says the change will make a big difference to the group’s venues.

Advertisement

“It’s super exciting and just in time for summer too,” he said. “I’m from the UK, so I grew up in Brighton and London, where it’s completely the norm to be outside the pub standing with a pint, with friends. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “On our busier days, like Anzac Day and during the sports season, our pubs are bursting at the seams, so this will give us more space, and it creates such a good energy to be able to have guests standing and drinking outside.” Publican James Wirth said drinking outdoors was part of the experience at the Old Fitzroy Hotel in Woolloomooloo. “At The Old Fitz and our other pubs, the pavement pint is half the point, and people standing outside on a warm summer’s evening is what people come here for, and it creates a really vibe-y atmosphere outside.” The Forrester’s in Surry Hills. In practice, the no-standing rule has not really been policed said Councillor Jess Miller. “As far as I’m aware, it’s never really been enforced. To the best of my knowledge, council has never walked up to a person and said, ‘excuse me, you need to sit down or find some furniture’.”

Instead, venues have been largely policing themselves so as not to be in breach of their licensing conditions. “We would ask people to find a table, and it’s never really been a comfortable conversation,” said Johnson. “It never really made sense to us, especially when our guests are just there trying to enjoy themselves with a drink and there’s only so many tables available.” The Old Fitzroy Hotel in Woolloomooloo. Janie Barrett Wirth said the rule was never enforced at The Old Fitz, where people regularly drink on the pavement, but he still welcomes the change. “It’s a small change, but council deserves credit for making it,” he said. “It speaks to the fact that council is listening and respecting how people want to use these areas, and recognise that vertical drinking isn’t a safety problem.”

Advertisement

The change does not alter how alcohol is sold or served, which must still comply with each venue’s liquor licence. Patrons can’t wander off with their drink from the venue’s designated outdoor dining areas, and standing is allowed only within its approved outdoor footprint. A clear path must also remain for pedestrians, wheelchairs and prams. The Shakey in Sydney’s Surry Hills. Miller says the bigger story is about $20 million in reforms, due to roll out over the next eight years, to expand outdoor dining spaces across Sydney. Pop-up dining spaces, such as those in carparks or on-street areas currently bordered by concrete barriers, will be made permanent, and footpaths will be extended to allow more people to be seated outside.

Work is expected to begin in the next few months, with extended outdoor dining areas planned for Glebe, Redfern, Surry Hills, Newtown and Erskineville. “Adding paving and landscaping, and making [a] permanent area outside of restaurants can effectively double their capacity, and that will have a huge impact on business,” said Miller.

PoliticsVictoriaHealthcare ‘System is in crisis’: Thousands of doctors to walk off the job over safety fears Melissa Cunningham Updated October 1, 2026 — 2:09pm ,first published 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of doctors from the state’s major hospitals will walk off the job on Thursday afternoon as part of their ongoing dispute with the government over pay and working conditions. Doctors will gather outside Parliament House in Melbourne to call for improvements to their working conditions including, a 30 per cent pay rise over four years, a cap of 12½ hours on shifts, paid overtime, and a guarantee of three consecutive days off during a fortnight of work. Doctors will walk off the job at several major public hospitals across Melbourne next week. Gabrielle Charotte The four-hour industrial action follows more than a year of strained negotiations with the Victorian government. Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation president Dr Roderick McRae said this week that working hours and fatigue among doctors in hospitals are so severe, they felt they had no option but to strike again.

Advertisement

“Our doctors do not take the decision to go on strike lightly,” McRae said. Related Article Healthcare Doctors to walk off job at major Melbourne hospitals over pay dispute “But the reality is they are being rostered on for 84-hour weeks and frequently work even longer when emergencies occur. They are often completely exhausted and burnt out, with little opportunity to rest between shifts. The threat that this systemic fatigue presents to patient safety is simply unacceptable.” Emergency departments would be exempt from the strike, McRae said, and staffing would remain above Saturday levels to ensure patient safety would not be put at risk. McRae said despite more than 14 months of negotiations and more than 60 meetings with three health ministers, the state government had failed to address doctors’ concerns.

Advertisement

“The Victorian hospital system is in crisis, and everyday patient safety is under threat.” He said doctors had already undertaken four separate strikes in specific regional and metropolitan locations. “Over the last six months, the government has repeatedly promised doctors that ‘an offer was imminent’,” McRae said. “But despite this, we’ve seen absolutely nothing put forward.” Non-critical and elective surgeries are expected to be delayed as a result of the mass walkout on Thursday afternoon. The government refused to answer questions about how many and which surgical and medical procedures would be impacted by the strike.

Advertisement

It has maintained there will be no impact to category 1 planned surgeries, which are critical and life-threatening cases. All hospitals affected have confirmed that they have safe staffing levels to deliver care to patients. Australian Medical Association Victoria president Dr Simon Judkins said doctors were not asking for anything unreasonable and simply wanted sustainable working conditions to protect patient welfare. “Doctors do not want to be attending protests,” he said. “They want to be in their hospitals doing what they’ve dedicated their lives to, and that’s caring for their patients.” He said that to ensure the best care for patients, Victorian doctors are asking for a 12½-hour limit to shifts and at least three guaranteed days off every fortnight to support proper rest and recovery.

Advertisement

“As other emergency services recognise, these basic measures are critical in managing fatigue and in keeping doctors and patients safe,” he said. Victorian Health Ingrid Stitt said every Victorian who turns up to a public hospital relied on the people working there. “We recognise the care and commitment they bring to their work,” she said. “We’ve been working directly with AMA and ASMOF, and discussions are progressing.” Stitt said patient care remained the government’s priority and hospitals were braced to manage any disruption.

title: Three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan retires a Lions legend
text:

Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan retires a Lions legend Peter Ryan Updated October 1, 2026 — 3:28pm ,first published 1:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Triple-premiership coach Chris Fagan has decided to retire as coach of the Brisbane Lions after leading the club to a historic third flag on Saturday. The 65-year-old told players and staff of his intentions at a meeting on Thursday afternoon ahead of the club’s best and fairest night. He departs on top with one year remaining on his contract, having coached the team into the past four grand finals for three premierships after taking the position in 2017 at the age of 55 when the Lions were second bottom on the ladder. Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan and co-captains Hugh McCluggage, Josh Dunkley and Harris Andrews with the premiership cup. AFL Photos Fagan coached the team to five wins in each of his first two seasons as coach before leading the club into the finals for the first time in 2019. They have not missed the finals since and achieved the three-peat with a remarkable comeback against Fremantle in Saturday’s grand final.

Advertisement

“As you’ve come to know I’ve been thinking about this for some time and I’m comfortable that now is the right time for [wife] Ursula and I to return to Melbourne to be closer to our family,” Fagan said in a statement. “Telling the players and football staff [on Thursday] was one of the hardest things I’ve done in my life. Together, we have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that. I was grateful to be given the role to coach the club, and it has been an incredible ride. “I especially want to thank Ursula and my daughters Jessica and Ellen for their incredible support over the journey, they have backed me through thick and thin. “This job is all encompassing; I’ve given it my absolute all and I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved, but now is the right time to go. “The boys will continue to contend, and I’ll be their No.1 fan, but a fresh face at the helm will be a key pillar for the players to come back to next season, as they work hard to achieve more success.

Advertisement

“I’ll miss the club and it will feel strange not to be involved but for the last 10 years I’ve thought about nothing other than how we can improve, get better and be successful. To see the club develop onfield from cellar dwellers to three-time premiers has been amazing. “The Lions are the sum of our parts and everyone across the club has played their role.” Lions chair Andrew Wellington expressed gratitude on behalf of the club not only to Fagan but his family, including his two daughters Jessica and Ellen. “He led with humility, without ego and with an unwavering commitment to helping those around him become better,” Wellington said. “His influence has reached far beyond the Brisbane Lions. Chris has helped strengthen football across Queensland, inspired a new generation of players and supporters, and earned the respect of the wider football public for the way he has carried himself through success and adversity.”

Advertisement

From Tasmania, Fagan, a premiership player with Hobart and Devonport, did not play football at the top level. He began his remarkable career as an administrator and coach when the late Neale Daniher appointed him to be Melbourne’s reserves coach in 1998. He then became an assistant coach at Hawthorn before progressing to become their football boss and was a key figure alongside senior coach Alastair Clarkson in the Hawks’ three-peat between 2013-15. Chris Fagan’s relationships with his players was a huge strength, and he also attracted players to the club. AFL Photos via Getty Images He left at the end of 2016 and then became embroiled in the AFL’s Hawthorn racism investigation, which ended up being resolved at the Human Rights Commission. The AFL found no adverse findings in relation to Fagan, who always denied wrongdoing, in their investigation, but the publicity took a toll on him. Fagan is now a legend at the Lions, standing alongside his mentor and friend, AFL legend Leigh Matthews as a triple-premiership Lions’ coach. His winning record in the past four seasons as coach of the Lions has been 70 per cent, but he has admitted at times he has felt more stress coaching a team in premiership contention than he did when the team was rebuilding.

Advertisement

It is likely the AFL’s incoming new club, the Tasmania Devils, will pursue Fagan to sit on their board as a director after he has a break. Fagan did not shy away from discussion that the grand final might be his final match as coach in the lead-up to the match and gave an indication as to which way he was leaning after the win. “It might sound like a strange thing for me to say after we just won a premiership, but I don’t really want to be that guy who hangs around until we fail,” he said. In a statement shared by the Lions, football manager Danny Daly said he would miss Fagan but was happy that he got to leave as a winner and on his own terms. “I’m forever grateful he backed me in to be the football manager, and I hope I have been able to repay him,” Daly said.

Advertisement

“The journey has been amazing, 10 years, eight finals campaigns, four grand finals and three premierships, it’s a record which over time we will come to appreciate a lot more. “I’m forever grateful that these aside, my family and I were able to be part of his and Ursula’s family life and forge a great and everlasting friendship.” Daly and assistant coach Cameron Bruce are among the potential candidates to replace Fagan. The Lions are expected to look broadly before they settle on a new coach. “Chris’ achievements speak for themselves, but his greatest legacy is the environment he created, the people he developed and how he has nurtured this playing group,” CEO Sam Graham said. “Today is a day to celebrate the contribution of Chris Fagan, Ursula and their family, and we will announce the next steps to appoint our next senior coach in due course.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet
text:
Advertisement

BusinessConsumer affairsPayments Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet Jessica Yun October 1, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Consumers and businesses are wrapping their heads around the Reserve Bank’s ban on card payment surcharges today and figuring out how it works. From October 1, you should no longer see an additional charge applied to card payments. If your coffee costs $5, that’s what you should expect to pay – at least, in theory. Card surcharges have been banned from October 1 onwards. Here’s what you need to know. Laurent Delhourme In practice, you may well still see a surcharge on your purchases as merchants and retailers adjust their approach. Here’s a quick cheat sheet on how the ban will work.

Advertisement

What has changed today? The Reserve Bank has changed the rules to now allow card networks – Mastercard, Visa and Eftpos – to ban surcharges for credit, debit and prepaid card payments made in store, online or via mobile wallets. PayPal, American Express, UnionPay are also removing surcharges from October 1. It means merchants are no longer allowed to charge an extra fee when you tap or insert your card at the point of sales, so the prices you see should be the price you pay. Retailers must clearly display how much an item or service costs with any applicable surcharge; so if you’re buying a $5 coffee, the displayed price should look like “$5.05 with card surcharge”. They must also disable surcharging on their terminals and take down any payment surcharge notices on display.

Advertisement

Behind the scenes, the new regime lowers processing costs for merchants by capping “interchange fees” – the fees paid between banks every time the customer taps or swipes their bank card. That fee goes from 0.8 per cent to a flat 0.3 per cent on Australian consumer credit cards. On domestic debit and prepaid cards, the ceiling has fallen from 10¢, or 0.2 per cent, to 8¢ or 0.16 per cent. Related Article Payments ‘Quite ill-prepared’: Shops scramble to meet new card surcharge ban What if I’m still being charged? Payment providers and banks have disabled the surcharge function on the terminals they control, but some older terminal machines don’t automatically update and may not yet reflect the changes. The RBA and the banking industry have urged patience as some businesses make the transition. Some business leaders have warned that some communities may not know about or understand the changes, particularly small business owners of migrant backgrounds or those who don’t speak English as a first language. The surcharge ban doesn’t include weekend and public holiday surcharges, which are still permitted.

Advertisement

Will businesses raise their prices? The short answer is: quite likely. These payment costs haven’t disappeared; they are just no longer allowed to appear as a separate charge. Most businesses are already facing and absorbing higher costs and overheads on many fronts and don’t feel able to absorb any more, so many will consider adjusting product or service prices and find savings elsewhere. How do I dispute surcharges? The ACCC and RBA can’t help you here – card networks (Visa, Mastercard and Eftpos) and payment providers (Square, Tyro, Stripe and some banks) – are in charge of enforcing the surcharge ban and will be held responsible if surcharges continue.

Advertisement

In the first instance, ask the merchant or retailer to clarify the surcharged amount (before payment if possible). Request a refund on the surcharged amount if necessary, and if they refuse, the next step is to report any unauthorised surcharges to your bank or card provider. The ACCC and state consumer protection agencies, such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria, will still be monitoring and enforcing consumer law to make sure businesses don’t mislead customers about prices or reasons for price rises. Should I pay in cash? The consumer watchdog has stated businesses are indeed allowed to offer discounts for a preferred payment method such as cash or PayID. “Payment method discounts should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay,” the ACCC states on its website.

Advertisement

We may well might start seeing more businesses, especially smaller ones, shifting back to cash as a result. According to Cash Welcome campaign manager Jason Bryce, this is already happening. Related Article Exclusive

Credit cards Surcharge ban could end popular free travel insurance perk “Most small retailers will raise prices to cover card costs and many will offer discounts for cash payments,” he said. So if you’re keen to save your dollars, keep some notes and coins on you. Will banks find a way to pass on the lost revenue? They already have, and not where you might expect to see it. Major banks have already wound back the generosity of credit card sign-on bonuses and rewards points earning rates, which were being funded by the higher interchange fees, and raising annual fees.

Advertisement

Commonwealth Bank has overhauled its loyalty program that pushes customers to spend rewards with Virgin’s Velocity scheme instead of Qantas Frequent Flyer points, and CBA customers who bundle multiple products, such as a mortgage or term deposits, will earn more points than those who have one account. Westpac has also announced fee hikes and cuts to benefits such as free travel insurance on its credit card line-up. NAB has made a number of changes that impact MyCard credit card holders (formerly Citibank cards) most dramatically; its premium “Prestige” card – which included 15 airport lounge visits, free hotel stay extensions and cashback on ride-shares, on top of generous points earning rates – has been scrapped entirely. American Express has also announced a scaling back of its airport lounge benefits. I’m a business owner. What should I do? It’s your responsibility to make sure you don’t continue to apply surcharges from today onwards. Get in touch with your bank or payment provider to implement the changes and update pricing details where you need to.

Advertisement

Shop around for the best deal. Corporate spending platform Archa’s chief executive Oliver Kidd recommends asking your card provider these questions: Has my points earn rate changed?

Have I lost any complimentary insurance?

Has my interest-free period changed?

Has my interest rate increased?

What am I really paying on foreign exchange fees, including any new mark-ups?

Has my credit limit changed without me knowing? “Business owners shouldn’t assume their card still offers the same value it did a year ago,” he said. If you’re looking more information, self-regulating body Australian Payments Network (AusPayNet) has put together an FAQ for consumers, businesses and payment providers at cardsurcharge.com.au. title: Want permanent residency in Japan? Here's how the rules are getting tougher
text:
In brief Foreigners seeking Japanese permanent residency will face tougher rules including higher fees.

The reforms are part of a tightening of immigration controls by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Japan has toughened requirements for foreigners seeking permanent residency as part of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to tighten immigration controls.

Under new rules that will come into effect in stages, foreign residents wishing to stay in Japan permanently will have to prove their annual income is above average and they can carry casual conversations in Japanese.

Application fees will also rise 20-fold from Thursday (from 10,000 yen ($91) to 200,000 yen ($1,800).

At one immigration office in central Tokyo visited by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency this week, hundreds of people queued, hoping to wrap up procedures before the price spike.

"I understand that over-accepting foreigners ... might dilute Japan's unique culture. But at the same time, given its low birth rate and aging population, Japan has to accept foreigners," said US-born university student Yujie Chono, who was among those waiting.

The 22-year-old told AFP, in fluent Japanese, that he had been waiting for five hours to file his paperwork.

Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills.

Even though Japan has a rapidly ageing population and is suffering labour shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.

"As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness," Takaichi said in an extended post on X on Sunday, adding that she was pushing for "orderly coexistence" with foreign nationals.

Programs to attract international workers have fuelled public worry.

Anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan go to foreigners and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.

Experts and many business leaders warn, however, that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.

Japan needs to open its doors to more foreigners, the Nikkei business daily said in a recent editorial.

"Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment," it said.

Anti-immigration sentiment

Foreigners were a major issue in last year's upper house election, which saw the sharp rise of the "Japanese-first" Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a "silent invasion".

The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs will be forced to leave Japan if they don't meet the new conditions.

Some foreign residents seek permanent residency to secure long-term stability, employment freedom and to earn trust within Japanese society. Those without permanent residency often have difficulty obtaining mortgages, for example.

Thursday's changes may prevent some people from applying for permanent residency but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.

Candidates must also show "understanding" of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

Having lived in Japan for a decade, permanent residency applicant Chono said he saw both sides of the debate but that the country needed young people "to support its future".

"In recent years, I believe there had been a strong push to promote cultural diversity. The momentum has stalled, perhaps, and maybe it may never fully return."

title: A buyer's market without buyers: Housing downturn deepens with nationwide falls
text:
in brief House prices have fallen 1.1 per cent in September, marking their sixth monthly decline.

The latest data from Cotality suggests widespread national downturn, rather than isolated declining regional markets.

Australian property values fell 1.1 per cent in September, dropping for the sixth consecutive month as the national housing downturn continues to pick up speed.

Cotality's latest home value index report shows overall property values are now 5.2 per cent lower than their March peak, with clearance rates faltering. Houses are sitting on the market for an average of 39 days across capital cities, up from 23 days a year ago.

The property market analysis firm's executive research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn reflects a "combination of affordability constraints," including higher interest rates, elevated living costs, and weaker consumer sentiment. All of these have "reduced purchasing capacity and dampened buyer demand", Lawless said.

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, bringing the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, in a bid to tackle persistent inflation. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows that borrowers are now spending an average of roughly $4,500 per month to service a standard 30-year loan.

"Borrowers are not only facing higher mortgage costs, but also an extended period of elevated living expenses and negative real income growth," Lawless said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Together, these pressures are narrowing the pool of buyers able to qualify for a mortgage and reducing the amount they can afford to pay."

Total advertised housing stock increased 23.1 per cent year-on-year, despite fresh listings entering the market, which dropped 9.2 per cent, as sales velocity declined.

"The lift in available stock is improving choice for buyers, but ironically, many prospective buyers don't have the confidence or financial capacity to buy at the moment," Lawless said.

A national downturn

While the market first showed signs of a downturn in the capital cities of Melbourne and Sydney, the scope and scale of the shift has widened to include virtually every market in the country.

In capital city suburbs, 97 per cent recorded a drop in dwelling values over the three months to the end of September. Every capital city recorded a monthly value fall in September, except Darwin, which rose 0.4 per cent.

In Sydney, housing values fell 1.4 per cent last month, and have dropped 8.6 per cent from their peak in February. The current pace of the decline is slightly faster than what was seen during the equivalent phase of the 2022-23 downturn.

"Sydney continues to lead the housing correction ... highlighting how rapid demand has weakened across the nation's largest housing market," Lawless said.

Melbourne property values dropped 0.7 per cent in September and are down 7.2 per cent below their November 2025 peak.

In regional areas, 71 per cent of local sub-markets dropped over the last month, falling 0.7 per cent. However, regional values remain 5.6 per cent higher annually.

Conditions shift in Brisbane

Brisbane saw the sharpest fall of all capital cities in September, dropping 1.5 per cent, outpacing Sydney's decline.

"The result highlights how sharply conditions have shifted in what had previously been one of the strongest performing housing markets," Lawless said.

Brisbane has overtaken Sydney as the capital city with the fastest declining property prices last month. Source: AAP / Jono Searle

Sales volumes have fallen the fastest in major cities which were previously growth leaders in the market. Brisbane is down 27.2 per cent, with Sydney just behind on 26.5 per cent and Perth at 24.2 per cent.

In mid-sized cities, the decline was less pronounced. Perth's home values have dropped 1.2 per cent over the past month while Adelaide fell 1.3 per cent.

Decline still has further to go

While the market is largely being driven by economic conditions, the Cotality report identifies changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax arrangements as having added "another layer of downside risk".

However, high construction costs, driven by inflationary pressures and labour force tightness, continue to suppress new housing supply, stabilising the market. Low unemployment rates are also preventing widespread selling, the report finds.

Speaking to ABC News on Thursday morning, Lawless said the property market is a buyer's market without buyers.

"Seller numbers are right down and I think that this really reflects the confidence in the housing market and the broader economy and cost of living pressures and high interest rates," he said. "So for now, even though it is a buyer's market, the missing piece of the puzzle is actually buyers."

Lawless pointed to the federal budget as having sent "a shudder" through the housing market, something Labor has frequently denied, and said that even bargain-hunters are staying away out of expectation that the market will continue to decline until interest rates drop.

The country's four largest trading banks all predict that interest rates will remain at their current level, if not higher, with the cycle starting to come down well into next year.

"It's pretty clear that headwinds facing demand are outweighing those supply-side challenges," Lawless said.

"That will be the case, I think, for at least going into 2027 — probably around the middle of next year."

title: Thriving Kids launches today. Here's what parents should know
text:
In brief The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended.

The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.

On 1 October, the first stage of Thriving Kids begins to roll out. This new program, announced just over a year ago, is part of the federal government’s sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

It means children aged eight and under, who have developmental delay or autism and low to moderate support needs, will increasingly receive support outside the NDIS, through Thriving Kids. The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.

But this doesn’t mean children are being moved off the NDIS today. Changes to NDIS access won't begin until January 2028.

So, what will Thriving Kids provide? And — after more than a year of negotiation, consultation and controversy — what questions remain?

How did we get here?

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended, and the scheme’s budget is growing too quickly.

One group the government says is particularly over-represented is children under 15. They make up just under half of all NDIS participants. One in two new entrants to the scheme is under nine — many with autism or developmental delay — and across the country one in ten six-year-olds receives NDIS support.

There is also mounting concern the scheme doesn’t serve all these young children well.

The government has argued these children would benefit more from strong, mainstream and community services, rather than an individual NDIS package.

But there wasn’t much initial detail

When Thriving Kids was announced in August 2025 there was relatively little detail. This caused considerable anxiety among families and disability advocates.

Since then — after an advisory process, a parliamentary inquiry, and lengthy negotiations between the Commonwealth and states and territories — we know more about the program.

The proposed national model will combine broad, or universal, supports with more targeted assistance for children who need additional help. Support will respond to children's needs rather than simply depend on a diagnosis, recognising that children's developmental and support needs are not static but can change over time.

So, how will Thriving Kids work?

Currently, children on the NDIS are assessed individually and receive a certain amount of funding their family can use to access services such as speech therapy or visits to a psychologist.

But Thriving Kids will provide supports where children are already going about their lives: in schools and early childhood centres, as well as community spaces (such as libraries or organised sport) and health care. These are known as foundational supports.

Some foundational supports will be universal, meaning they are available to all children and families. These include providing information about child development and linking families to services.

Some universal supports will begin on 1 October — such as supported playgroups for children aged five and under — or shortly after, such as the Medicare-funded health check for three-year-olds, done by GPs and rolling out in November.

Some supports will be targeted to kids' specific needs and provided by allied health professionals, such as occupational therapists, speech pathologists and physiotherapists. These will require some form of assessment to access.

Children with permanent and significant disability, including children with high support needs, will continue to be eligible for the NDIS.

State and territory governments will take the lead on designing and commissioning services that are appropriate to their local population. But Queensland is yet to sign up, so important questions remain about how this will work.

What have some of the sticking points been?

Important questions about Thriving Kids' implementation remain.

One of the biggest challenges has been working out who is responsible for providing and paying for supports outside the NDIS. This problem predates Thriving Kids.

In 2023, the NDIS Review argued the NDIS had blown out its estimates so much because states and territories had moved away from providing disability supports, forcing people to seek NDIS support.

Foundational supports — jointly funded by all governments — are meant to be part of the solution. Thriving Kids is the first program of this kind to be launched.

But while states and territories initially signed up to the federal government’s new model, the relationship has become more fractious as plans have developed.

And while the other states and territories have signed on to deliver Thriving Kids and are developing plans about what these will look like in their communities, Queensland is yet to sign up.

At the moment we don’t know what this will mean for younger children with low-to-moderate needs in Queensland. For example, some aspects of Thriving Kids’ first stage will be rolled out, focusing on general supports. But it’s unclear whether targeted services will be developed.

What do we still need to know?

The Queensland minister for disability services, Amanda Camm, has previously said the federal government has not sufficiently defined what it means by developmental delay or different levels of support needs. She argues the federal government simply wants to shift costs to the states and territories.

The Queensland government shares a concern with a number of disability advocates: that children and families might fall between gaps in services if they’re no longer eligible for the NDIS but can’t get the specific support they need through Thriving Kids.

NDIS eligibility is set to tighten, with the government seeking to cut 160,000 participants from the scheme over the next four years.

So what will happen for families whose children age out of Thriving Kids — at nine — but aren’t eligible for NDIS support? This is a key concern.

The kind of early intervention offered by Thriving Kids is important, but for most children their support needs won’t disappear as they age.

The government has floated the idea of a Thriving Teens scheme, but there are no solid plans yet.

What happens next?

This first stage of Thriving Kids focuses on general universal supports, such as information and advice for families who have concerns about their child’s development, and supported playgroups for children aged five and under.

From January 2027, states and territories will start to develop and roll out targeted supports. These are for children who need additional support, for example, low-cost assistive technologies or speech therapy.

The NDIS will not change its eligibility criteria until January 2028, meaning children will continue to be admitted to the scheme until these changes take place.

Catherine Smith is a senior lecturer of wellbeing science at the Melbourne Graduate School of Education at the University of Melbourne. She receives funding from the NDRP and Australian governments.

title: 'We don't understand': Little-noticed change could hit millions of Australian websites
text:
in brief New rules that could make it more difficult to register .com.au websites have been proposed.

However, other experts suggest the changes will not be as dramatic as they are being made out to be.

A quiet policy shift within Australia's web address regulatory body has industry experts concerned that millions of local websites could be pushed offline, even as the government urges a wait-and-see approach.

Last month, the board of the .au Domain Administrator (auDA) approved "in-principle" recommendations from an independent panel that would overhaul eligibility rules for domestic website registrations.

The decision, recently announced by auDA, will see the long-standing "close and substantial connection" rule scrapped. Companies and organisations will soon no longer be able to register web addresses based on products, services, or events, but will instead have to link their websites to their name alone.

Domain industry experts estimate that "potentially millions" of Australian websites could be impacted and that "confidence" in the .com.au domain address could be shaken if the proposed changes go ahead.

auDA said in a statement to SBS News that rule changes have yet to be finalised and that "most" domain name holders are expected to meet the new requirements.

Under the current rules, businesses are allowed to register website names that are related to their services — such as applepies.com.au for a bakery — but under the new rules, they could need a much more closely aligned Australian company name to match the site.

"The independent review recommendation is intended to strengthen the connection between a com.au or net.au domain name and the domain name holder's official business identity, helping maintain the trust Australians place in .au domain names," the auDa statement said.

"The Panel found the current criteria can create inconsistency in how the allocation rules are applied, can be seen as unfair to small businesses, and in some instances may result in consumer harm."

'More red tape'

Former auDa chair and domain lawyer Erhan Karabardak voted against the change on the divided advisory panel. He said the policy "throws the baby out with the bathwater" and will fail to address the problem it was designed to.

"We still don't understand what the justification was," Karabardak said.

He said the policy change stems from a desire to curb domain investors and "monetised" web portfolios from claiming generic domain names to sell them to legitimate businesses.

However, he argued commercial domain investors will simply work around the change by registering multi-word business names with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and that everyday users will end up paying more.

"Whenever a business wants to register a generic name, product, or service, they're going to have to firstly pay for a business name — $47 a year — and then pay for a domain name," he said. "It's effectively doubling the cost of registering a .com.au or .net.au domain name."

Schools, charities, and small businesses that want a temporary domain name to promote an event could struggle to do so under the new rules.

Registrants will see the process as "more red tape" and opt to use a different domain address like .com where there are fewer rules, Karabardak said.

Improving trust in the age of AI

While the announcement of the change has sparked concern among industry insiders, some have urged caution until the full details are known.

Patrick Myles, an independent domain industry consultant, told SBS News that he expects the number of registrants who might be impacted will be "pretty small" and that updates to business organisational practices are a routine part of day-to-day operations.

"I'm in this category myself," Myles said. "I have multiple domains, and some of them are less associated with my business than others so [the changes] might impact me a bit, but it doesn't worry me at all."

READ MORE OpenAI apologises for AI models that breached Australian government websites

In an era of declining trust in global institutions and declining relevance of domain names as artificial intelligence changes how users access the internet, Myles said protection of national domain names is increasingly important.

"If you don't support the policies around your country code ... it basically becomes existential," Myles said.

Myles, who has worked for auDA previously, said the changes proposed are "one of the best ways to ensure that the brand of .au is retained and it is kept as strong as it can be in a very, very cloudy world".

While the requirements for registering a .com.au domain could become stricter, Myles advises anyone who fails to meet the new standards to register an .au address, which has fewer requirements.

title: Rates were this high 15 years ago. Here's why it hurts more now
text:
IN BRIEF The size of the average home loan has greatly increased since 2011.

Economists say that while interest rate hikes hurt, high inflation would have worse implications.

When the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) lifted the cash rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6 per cent, it brought interest rates to their highest in 15 years.

The economic climate in 2011 was vastly different to today and interest rates are about where the comparison ends.

The average home loan has more than doubled since then, and the average house price has increased from 115 to 130 per cent, varying by state and territory.

Richard Holden, professor of economics at the University of New South Wales, said rising property prices meant households were carrying more debt on average.

"Any given increase in interest rates has much more of an effect than it did 15 years ago," he told SBS News.

"The Reserve Bank seems to have really pivoted to tackling inflation more seriously, and that's going to take most likely another couple of rate rises ... it's just the beginning of more pain for those households."

Wages haven't moved at the same pace as rising house prices and the cost of entering the market has exploded.

The average mortgage in 2011 was equivalent to around 5.4 years of average full-time earnings, while it's now closer to 6.7 years.

In 2011, the average loan size for a first-home buyer was $281,100, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Changes to the ABS data collection for Housing Finance data were made in 2019, producing a "level shift" in the available historical data. The ABS said the figures "remained conceptually similar to those published in the existing publication, but with improved quality". Source: SBS News

In 2026, that figure is $731,000, ranging from $516,000 on average in Tasmania to $842,000 in NSW, according to ABS and Canstar data.

House prices have surged due to a number of factors — RBA researchers have found that increases are driven by demand that consistently outstrips supply.

In a 2024 report, RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter pointed to population growth as a factor contributing to this demand, calling for a "balancing" of the scales.

But there has been growing interest in how negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts in housing influenced the steep incline in housing prices this century, a hypothesis supported in a 2024 study from the University of New South Wales.

The current average variable rate is between 6.24 and 6.62 per cent for owner-occupiers, meaning the average Australian is spending $4,500 to $4,680 per month on their mortgage.

READ MORE The numbers every mortgage borrower and hopeful buyer should know

Assuming banks pass on the change in full, Canstar predicts the average owner-occupier variable rate will climb to 6.49 per cent.

In that case, it isn't just homeowners with mortgages who are impacted — Holden said that while it was difficult to determine due to many competing factors, there was anecdotal evidence suggesting interest rate hikes can be passed down from borrowers to renters.

A 'very different' economy

Warwick McKibbin, emeritus professor of economics and public policy at the Australian National University, says that unlike in 2011, this month's hike comes at a time of high uncertainty for the global economy.

"It's very different," he told SBS News, pointing to what he described as "large waste" in government revenue accumulated amid Australia's early 2000s resources boom, when mining investment surged from historical averages of 1.5 per cent to 9 per cent of GDP by 2012.

"Instead of being saved, like the Norwegians did with their sovereign wealth fund, with all the revenue from the oil boom going into a sovereign wealth fund, we just spent it on government outlays and subsidies."

Because of this, McKibbin said, Australia was now in a "much worse" economic position, in which the pressure of high interest rates would fall on both borrowers and the government.

"We had that opportunity to reduce debt to much lower levels, and we didn't. Now, the government has to service its debt, which is now much larger than it was in 2011."

The RBA has delivered four consecutive interest rate hikes this year, in a bid to bring inflation down.

On Wednesday, Australia's annual headline inflation rate jumped to 4 per cent for the 12 months to August 2026, up 0.5 per cent since July.

McKibbin says regardless of any pain caused by high interest rates, the consequences of high inflation were "far worse".

"Mortgage holders will have to pay more, and mortgages are much bigger than they were back in 2011. So the impact on their individual household budget is going to be more severe."

But, he said, it was dangerous to look in isolation at who was going to lose, especially in the face of high inflation and its impact on cost of living pressures for people at the lower end of the income scale.

While interest rates would impact many households, McKibbin said Australians would overwhelmingly benefit from inflation coming down and cost increases slowing.

"The reality is that interest rates have to go up when there's too much demand in the economy, and these federal and state governments are responsible," he said.

"It's important that this is done. And the reasons for doing it must be understood by the Australian public."

Holden agreed, saying: "Higher interest payments are going to be tough.

"But if we don't get inflation under control, that really hurts everybody, particularly those at the lower end of the income distribution."

title: Australia's card surcharge ban starts today. Here's everything you need to know
text:
in brief The surcharge ban covers eftpos, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

From today, the familiar sting of a card surcharge will disappear for Australians paying with most major cards.

But the changes come with a few catches — and not every checkout fee is going away.

Here’s what consumers need to know.

What exactly changes from today?

From 1 October, businesses can no longer add a separate surcharge simply because a customer pays by card on the affected payment networks.

The change comes through new no-surcharge rules introduced by the card networks and follows a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.

In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, that's the price you'll pay and you should no longer see an extra card-payment fee added when you tap or insert your card.

Which cards and payment methods are covered?

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.

The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.

Does the ban apply online as well as in-store?

Yes. The change is about the payment method, not whether you are standing at a shop counter or buying from a website.

So an online retailer cannot simply retain a separate Visa, Mastercard or EFTPOS card surcharge because the transaction happens online. The same principle applies to card payments made through apps and other digital checkout systems.

Can businesses still charge booking fees, service fees or weekend surcharges?

Yes, as the RBA site explained: "The changes only apply to surcharges added because a customer pays by card."

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

Will this make paying cheaper?

The end of surcharges does not necessarily mean lower prices.

Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but what's changing is they can no longer add them as an extra fee. They may choose to incorporate them into the total price.

The RBA says, "those costs can be reflected in a business’s overall pricing, rather than charged as a separate surcharge".

Could businesses raise prices instead?

Yes. Businesses are generally free to set and change their prices, as long as they do not mislead customers.

READ MORE How to slash your bills and get money back into your pocket quickly

That means a cafe, retailer, or professional service could increase its standard price to cover payment-processing costs.

Can businesses set minimum spends or stop accepting cards?

Businesses can choose which payment methods they accept and can set minimum card-payment amounts, subject to applicable rules.

So don't assume every business will have to accept your card simply because surcharges are disappearing.

Can businesses offer discounts for paying by cash or another method?

Yes. Businesses can encourage customers to use another payment method by offering a discount rather than imposing a card surcharge.

For example, a business could offer a discount for paying by cash or PayID.

What should you do if you’re still charged a card surcharge?

The consumer watchdog has advice for customers who suspect they've been hit with a card surcharge.

First, check what the fee actually is. It may be a legitimate booking, service or weekend surcharge rather than a card-payment surcharge.

If it appears to be a card surcharge, raise it with the business and ask them to remove the fee or refund it.

"Businesses shouldn’t try to avoid the 'no surcharge' rules … by describing a card payment surcharge as another type of fee or charge," the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said on its website.

From 1 October, consumers can also raise concerns with the relevant card network or the business's payment provider and can report potentially misleading pricing to the ACCC or their state or territory consumer protection agency.

title: The grand 'chonkion' of this year's Fat Bear Week has been declared
text:

Backpack, officially known as Bear 89, received over 100,000 votes to become the 2026 winner.

Backpack has emerged victorious as this year's Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear in Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.

The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, was declared the winner on Wednesday AEST with more than 100,000 votes, narrowly beating Bear 910 with just over 50 per cent of the poll.

The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state's south-west corner toward the Aleutian Islands.

Fat Bear Week was established in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies.

The 2025 winner, Chunk — officially known as Bear 32 — clinched his victory at an estimated 545kg.

title: How one pensioner's eviction became a flashpoint in Spain's housing crisis
text:
In brief Spain’s government proposed banning evictions until 2030 and curbing property speculation amid a housing crisis.

An 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked protests accepted a deal to return to her home.

Spain's coalition government said it had agreed to proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country's housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests accepted an offer to return home.

Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid's main squares on Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal's removal from her home on a stretcher last week. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.

Spanish health minister Monica Garcia said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement with junior partner Sumar on Tuesday for a set of new measures, including rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market.

However, the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented parliament.

The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation, housing minister Isabel Rodriguez told a news conference, naming Urbagestion, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.

Urbagestion didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted on in parliament later this week, with the majority in a first decree. The "final sticking point" of automatic contract rollover is in a second decree, social affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy told a news conference.

'Time to intervene'

"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," Garcia said in a post on X.

Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.

"We all agreed that evictions — where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros — obviously need to be stopped," Junts parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said on RTVE.

"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property — putting them all in the same basket — is a mistake," she added.

Madrid's tenants' union criticised the government's decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned.

The lawyer for pensioner Abascal said on Tuesday that Urbagestion, the fund that owns her apartment, had offered a preliminary agreement that will allow her return to her home, paying 30 per cent of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 ($811) a month.

This would see her paying at a similar level to before the eviction.

"She should never have been forced to leave," Beatriz Duro told reporters. "I hope this case serves to provide a collective response to the housing crisis."
