title: 'Grading each other's homework': AI industry CEOs bow to Trump-led push for self-regulation
text:
In brief Donald Trump said leading AI companies had signed a "morally binding" pact to self-regulate and improve safeguards.

Tech leaders backed stronger oversight measures, but debate over AI risks and regulation remained unresolved.

United States President Donald Trump says the tech executives who gathered at the White House on Wednesday to discuss regulating AI had signed a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards for the fast-moving technology.

"They're going to police themselves," Trump said after the meeting that gathered the top leaders in artificial intelligence, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

Trump said the tech bosses had signed a deal that would put on paper their commitment to self-regulate in a morally binding agreement that would not be legally enforceable.

But the final document, dubbed the White House Accord, left the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations" if it made sense over time.

Speaking to reporters outside the Oval Office surrounded by the world's most powerful tech bosses, Trump also confirmed that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence "because it's not artificial".

Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg said the accord aims to assure customers that AI technology "works in the way that we intend".

The commitment includes "robust internal controls" and multiple layers of auditing — from internal risk reviews to external auditors and oversight from the companies' boards of directors, he said.

Zuckerberg called it a starting point for industry-wide standards.

Elon Musk said the executives essentially agreed to "grading each other's homework, which is a lot better than if people just grade their own homework, for obvious reasons".

The lunch meeting also included Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Sundar Pichai of Google.

READ MORE OpenAI apologises for AI models that breached Australian government websites

Of the 31 guests, two were women: Susie Wiles, Donald Trump's chief of staff, and Lisa Su, CEO of semiconductor company AMD.

The gathering occurred as attitudes toward AI sour in Washington DC, with politicians increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow AI development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.

Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which OpenAI's autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, starting with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

OpenAI announced on Tuesday that it was cancelling the release of its latest model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the ChatGPT-maker revealed it did not meet safety standards.

Trump, advised by Huang and his former AI czar David Sacks, has urged unfettered AI development to outpace China and fuel a US economy increasingly dependent on AI-driven growth.

The issue of data centres, the vast computing facilities the technology requires, has emerged as a flashpoint in midterm election races in both parties, with more and more communities worried about rising electricity bills and the strain on water and land.

Trump has dismissed opponents of these data centres and, after the meeting, insisted that AI companies "will be very generous" with communities who open their doors to them.

"They'll help with their schools, they'll help with their teachers," he said.

'Still under discussion'

Major AI companies, particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, have issued stark public warnings about uncontrolled development of increasingly powerful systems — even as they develop and deploy this same state-of-the-art technology.

Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.

Anthropic warned investors of potential existential risks to humanity in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

Anthropic is aiming for an IPO as early as November.

Trump has repeatedly characterised these warnings about existential risks as overblown, and the White House has bitterly clashed with Anthropic over AI safety.

"As the president has said, whoever wins AI, wins. I think that's very important," Amodei said after the meeting. "But I think the technology has very real risks, and the mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion."

title: Socceroos shine bright and fizzle out in action-packed clash with Brazil in Brisbane
text:
In brief The Socceroos went down 4-2 to Brazil in their second friendly match.

After a muscular first half that rattled Brazil's cage, the Australian defence couldn't hold the visitors at bay.

A fired-up Brazil team has outgunned the Socceroos 4-2 in a dramatic rematch in which the hosts held a brief lead thanks to a Connor Metcalfe stunner.

A 1-1 draw in Townsville on Friday clearly stirred five-time World Cup champions Brazil.

The Brazilians scored in the third minute on Tuesday and, after a fiery tussle that spilled onto the Socceroos' bench, found two late goals to secure victory in front of a sell-out 52,423-strong Lang Park crowd.

Australia led until the final play in Townsville and will leave Brisbane frustrated after again throwing away good chances to notch a famous victory.

But, ahead of January's Asian Cup, the "brave", incisive shifts under coach Tony Popovic since the World Cup bode well.

"Went behind early ... you're playing Brazil, and we responded in a fantastic manner," Popovic said.

"Up until they scored the third goal we were very much in the match, had chances of our own."

The Socceroos hadn't even completed a pass when Brazil's Vanderson threaded a shot from the corner of the box to finish some neat build-up and open their account.

Goalkeeper Patrick Beach saved the Socceroos' blushes with back-to-back blocks on efforts by Raphinha moments later.

But after that early pressure, the hosts settled in and threw punches of their own, a display of creative passing from Jackson Irvine consistently putting Nestory Irankunda into dangerous spaces.

Tete Yengi held the ball up well and kept Australia pressing.

The reply came in the 28th minute from Alessandro Circati, with the tall defender scrambling a close-range goal from a corner.

Then Connor Metcalfe, who had expertly delivered for Circati, put Australia ahead emphatically.

Camped outside the box, he defied a lack of time and space to curl a left-footer into the top-right corner and cue delirium from the sell-out crowd at Lang Park.

Gaps remained in a Brazilian unit, arguably rattled, as coach Carlo Ancelotti remonstrated with the sideline official when Gabriel was booked for tagging Yengi's foot.

The visitors only trailed for 10 minutes, though. Harry Souttar downed Danilo Santos in the box and Barcelona star Raphina drove home the resultant penalty.

Irankunda was gifted another late chance in the final seconds of a frenetic first half, but smoked his shot over the bar when Brazil keeper Otavio Costa's attempted clearance was delivered to his feet.

Tensions built then flared with a series of fouls each way, Irankunda earning a yellow for a nasty-looking effort on Danilo.

Australia kept coming and in the 61st minute should have nipped ahead again when Circati put his close-range header from another well-taken corner over the bar.

Minutes later, things threatened to become ugly when a heated tussle between Souttar and Endrick spilled to the sideline in front of the Australian bench. Both were given a yellow for their troubles.

Endrick had the last laugh, though, laying on an assist for Bruno Guimaraes almost instantly after play restarted.

Beach's outstretched left hand then denied a further goal in the 76th minute.

The fourth wasn't far behind though, with Irankunda making enough contact just inside the box to fell Vinicius Junior, who sneaked his penalty kick into the left corner.

Brisbane teenager Lucas Herrington watched his late chance to get the Socceroos within a goal slide by the left post.

"Great, entertaining, open game," Ancelotti, who admitted his surprise at the Socceroos' press, pressure and organisation, said.

title: Australia is closing in on the world's highest rates. Only one country is in front
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's cash rate is now one of the highest in the world, but lower than Iceland's.

Experts say Iceland's dramatic rate is the product of over two decades of financial instability.

Australia has the second-highest interest rate among comparable economies after the Reserve Bank hiked rates to a 15-year high on Tuesday.

Taking the crown is Iceland, where the cash rate currently sits at 8 per cent — the highest of the 41 advanced economies as defined by the International Monetary Fund.

The Central Bank of Iceland set the historic rate in August, claiming the increase was "driven mainly by hikes in public levies and price increases caused by the war in the Middle East".

Similarly, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cited higher energy and fuel prices and the Middle East conflict as reasons for Australia's hike from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers denied a fair comparison could be made between Australia and Iceland's interest rates.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"If you want to make a comparison with other countries and other economies, you need to acknowledge that growth here is faster than a lot of other economies," he said on Tuesday following the RBA announcement.

Chalmers said Australia currently has fast economic and employment growth, low debt and an economy "equal to the US".

"We've got a lot going for us in Australia, but we've got a lot coming at us from around the world as well — that's clear in the Reserve Bank's Statement," he said.

"We take all of those challenges very seriously. When you compare us to the world, there are some things that we are doing much better than the rest of the world."

Source: SBS News

Iceland, a small island nation that sits between Greenland and Norway in the Atlantic Ocean, has a population of almost 397,000 — almost 100,000 less than the ACT.

As of August, the national inflation rate was 5.6 per cent.

"While it does have considerable supplies of renewable geothermal energy ... it's reliant on transporting almost everything other than the food it can grow for itself," independent economist Saul Eslake told SBS News.

"It's very exposed to the increases in energy prices that we have seen since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East."

Eslake explained that Iceland's high interest rate can be attributed to a "fairly tumultuous" 25 years.

"It had an enormous boom in the lead-up to the global financial crisis of 2007/8. But then, Iceland faced the collapse of its banking system and house prices, and large parts of its economy."

He said Iceland had one of the most traumatic experiences of any country during the global financial crisis.

"That left Iceland more vulnerable than other economies might be to the kind of shocks that we've seen this year."

He said one of the major mistakes the Central Bank of Iceland made was decreasing interest rates as inflation unexpectedly rose after the COVID-19 pandemic.

"They pushed up their cash rate to 11 per cent in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic because inflation rose more than almost any other country," he said.

"They then cut interest rates in 2023, and cut them back down to 9.25 per cent in 2025 — only to find that inflation didn't fall, it rose again.

This followed further interest rate rises to tackle inflation.

Eslake said the RBA made the same mistake in 2025 when it didn't increase interest rates and so, in the face of rising inflation, was forced to increase rates in February this year.

In August, Iceland's government held a referendum on negotiating membership in the European Union, which would include replacing its Króna currency with the euro, and potentially easing financial pressure.

The European Central Bank interest rate is 2.25 per cent compared to Iceland's 8 per cent.

"It would not solve Iceland's structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy," Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson, chief economist at Icelandic labour union Viska, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

However, Iceland voted 52.8 per cent against the referendum's proposal. Instead, the nation's government will focus on strengthening its ties with the EU through the European Economic Area Agreement, which it shares with Norway and Liechtenstein.

Eslake was unsurprised by the verdict, believing Iceland a proud nation.

"Clearly, Icelanders value their independence," he said.

As for Australia, Eslake said Tuesday's interest rate hike was "entirely expected".

"It flows from the stronger-than-expected inflation data that we've seen over the past couple of months. It flows from the fact that most indicators for economic activity have been a little stronger than expected," he said.

"As the Reserve Bank board said today, it also reflects the renewed increases in energy prices as a result of the ongoing impasse or conflict in the Middle East, which is not looking likely to last much longer than anticipated."

Eslake said it isn't a fair or appropriate comparison to link Australia and Iceland.

"We are very different countries, with very different trading relationships and very different economic structures as well as being very different in scale and scope," he said.

However, the economist warned that both Iceland's Central Bank and the RBA should be more careful when betting on falling inflation.

"You don't want to be in an embarrassing position to reverse the interest rate cuts that you've previously instituted," he said.

"You have to have good reason to be confident you're on top of the inflation problem you're seeking to solve before cutting interest rates."

title: What's worrying the RBA now? The risks it couldn't ignore
text:
Key Points The RBA has raised interest rates to address "three big risks".

An economist says there are already indications of another rate raise at the board's next meeting in November.

The head of the Reserve Bank hopes the fourth rate rise of the year announced on Tuesday will turn the tide on the past six months of elevated inflation.

The RBA announced interest rates would rise to 4.6 per cent from 4.35 per cent and didn’t rule out a potential fifth rate rise this year in November to try to tame inflation.

"The hope here is that this will be restrictive enough," Michele Bullock told reporters on Tuesday afternoon. "Now, will it be enough? I don't know."

The rate rise follows six months of underlying inflation of around 3.5 per cent, above the board's target range of 2-3 per cent.

The RBA's mandate is to reduce inflation into this band, while protecting as many jobs as it can.

'Three big risks'

In justifying the call to increase rates, Bullock said the effect of the first three rate rises this year are still flowing through.

However, "three big risks" have also started to materialise over this time.

"One was the Middle East conflict going on for longer and fuel prices rising again," she said, citing previous guidance which had predicted that oil and energy prices would have stabilised by now.

The second challenge, according to Bullock, is the "AI boom", which was adding to demand both in Australia and overseas, although she said the risk had not fully materialised.

This boom has partly driven up prices for technology-related goods.

Finally she said domestic capacity pressures were higher than anticipated, referring to an economic situation where too much money is chasing too few goods.

"It's difficult to estimate output gaps and how tight the labour market is," she acknowledged, explaining that inflation numbers and unit labour costs come into play.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics is due to release the latest inflation figures on Wednesday morning.

Will there be another rate rise this year?

Several key economic indicators will be released before the RBA meets again in November, giving policymakers more data to assess the inflation outlook.

However, major bank ANZ is already predicting interest rates will then rise to 4.85 per cent.

Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said there are already indications the board could hike rates again.

"For starters, the Board's decision was unanimous. The Board also explicitly warned that it may raise rates again if needed," he said in a statement.

"Ominously, the Bank noted that local firms are facing higher costs and are either raising prices or "looking to do so". This suggests that inflation could rise even further in the months ahead."

Bullock declined to predict what the board would decide at its next meeting in November, saying the RBA will do what it has to do to reduce inflation.

"But if we can avoid massive job losses and a massive increase in the unemployment rate, that is a really important thing to be able to try and do."

title: Three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan retires a Lions legend

Triple-premiership coach Chris Fagan has decided to retire as coach of the Brisbane Lions after leading the club to a historic third flag on Saturday. The 65-year-old told players and staff of his intentions at a meeting on Thursday afternoon ahead of the club’s best and fairest night. He departs on top with one year remaining on his contract, having coached the team into the past four grand finals for three premierships after taking the position in 2017 at the age of 55 when the Lions were second bottom on the ladder. Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan and co-captains Hugh McCluggage, Josh Dunkley and Harris Andrews with the premiership cup. AFL Photos Fagan coached the team to five wins in each of his first two seasons as coach before leading the club into the finals for the first time in 2019. They have not missed the finals since and achieved the three-peat with a remarkable comeback against Fremantle in Saturday’s grand final.

Advertisement

“As you’ve come to know I’ve been thinking about this for some time and I’m comfortable that now is the right time for [wife] Ursula and I to return to Melbourne to be closer to our family,” Fagan said in a statement. “Telling the players and football staff [on Thursday] was one of the hardest things I’ve done in my life. Together, we have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that. I was grateful to be given the role to coach the club, and it has been an incredible ride. “I especially want to thank Ursula and my daughters Jessica and Ellen for their incredible support over the journey, they have backed me through thick and thin. “This job is all encompassing; I’ve given it my absolute all and I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved, but now is the right time to go. “The boys will continue to contend, and I’ll be their No.1 fan, but a fresh face at the helm will be a key pillar for the players to come back to next season, as they work hard to achieve more success.

Advertisement

“I’ll miss the club and it will feel strange not to be involved but for the last 10 years I’ve thought about nothing other than how we can improve, get better and be successful. To see the club develop onfield from cellar dwellers to three-time premiers has been amazing. “The Lions are the sum of our parts and everyone across the club has played their role.” Lions chair Andrew Wellington expressed gratitude on behalf of the club not only to Fagan but his family, including his two daughters Jessica and Ellen. “He led with humility, without ego and with an unwavering commitment to helping those around him become better,” Wellington said. “His influence has reached far beyond the Brisbane Lions. Chris has helped strengthen football across Queensland, inspired a new generation of players and supporters, and earned the respect of the wider football public for the way he has carried himself through success and adversity.”

Advertisement

From Tasmania, Fagan, a premiership player with Hobart and Devonport, did not play football at the top level. He began his remarkable career as an administrator and coach when the late Neale Daniher appointed him to be Melbourne’s reserves coach in 1998. He then became an assistant coach at Hawthorn before progressing to become their football boss and was a key figure alongside senior coach Alastair Clarkson in the Hawks’ three-peat between 2013-15. Chris Fagan’s relationships with his players was a huge strength, and he also attracted players to the club. AFL Photos via Getty Images He left at the end of 2016 and then became embroiled in the AFL’s Hawthorn racism investigation, which ended up being resolved at the Human Rights Commission. The AFL found no adverse findings in relation to Fagan, who always denied wrongdoing, in their investigation, but the publicity took a toll on him. Fagan is now a legend at the Lions, standing alongside his mentor and friend, AFL legend Leigh Matthews as a triple-premiership Lions’ coach. His winning record in the past four seasons as coach of the Lions has been 70 per cent, but he has admitted at times he has felt more stress coaching a team in premiership contention than he did when the team was rebuilding.

Advertisement

It is likely the AFL’s incoming new club, the Tasmania Devils, will pursue Fagan to sit on their board as a director after he has a break. Fagan did not shy away from discussion that the grand final might be his final match as coach in the lead-up to the match and gave an indication as to which way he was leaning after the win. “It might sound like a strange thing for me to say after we just won a premiership, but I don’t really want to be that guy who hangs around until we fail,” he said. In a statement shared by the Lions, football manager Danny Daly said he would miss Fagan but was happy that he got to leave as a winner and on his own terms. “I’m forever grateful he backed me in to be the football manager, and I hope I have been able to repay him,” Daly said.

“The journey has been amazing, 10 years, eight finals campaigns, four grand finals and three premierships, it’s a record which over time we will come to appreciate a lot more. “I’m forever grateful that these aside, my family and I were able to be part of his and Ursula’s family life and forge a great and everlasting friendship.” Daly and assistant coach Cameron Bruce are among the potential candidates to replace Fagan. The Lions are expected to look broadly before they settle on a new coach. “Chris’ achievements speak for themselves, but his greatest legacy is the environment he created, the people he developed and how he has nurtured this playing group,” CEO Sam Graham said. “Today is a day to celebrate the contribution of Chris Fagan, Ursula and their family, and we will announce the next steps to appoint our next senior coach in due course.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. A fiery five-hour council meeting took a personal turn when the Woollahra mayor revealed she looked up the value of a pro-housing advocate’s home during a debate over plans to add 9400 homes to Sydney’s eastern suburbs. There was only one item on the agenda at Woollahra Council’s extraordinary meeting on Wednesday night – to finalise how the council would respond to the most significant rezoning of the eastern suburbs in decades. Under state government plans unveiled last month, housing density would be concentrated around Woollahra and Edgecliff train stations, building towers up to 32 and 34 storeys. One admission tipped the temperature inside Woollahra Council’s chambers almost to boiling point. Wolter Peeters More than 10 pro-housing advocates spoke at the public forum and were met with staunch opposition and questioning from some of the 13 councillors who attended. The meeting featured numerous interjections and tetchy back-and-forth exchanges, and multiple points of order were called. At one point, Liberal mayor Sarah Dixson said she was “one word away” from calling an adjournment to turn the temperature down. About 40 minutes into the five-hour-long meeting, it was a personal question that almost tipped the temperature in the room to boiling point.

Advertisement

It began when councillor Mary-Lou Jarvis asked Sydney YIMBY’s chair Justin Simon if he could afford to buy a freestanding house with a median price of $5.4 million in Elizabeth Bay, quoting figures from realestate.com.au. “I could not afford to buy a house in Woollahra [council area] anywhere,” Simon responded. Loading Dixson interjected and revealed she had looked up Simon’s home address before he spoke at the meeting: “Hang on, I mean, I’ve looked at the cost of your house, and you certainly could afford to, you certainly could. “The cost of his home, according to realestate.com, is more than the average price in Woollahra.”

Advertisement

Simon’s reaction was one of disbelief: “Sorry, so the cost of my home ... So you’ve taken my address that I signed up for to speak at council, and you’ve then gone and looked up my home on realestate.com? That’s such a bizarre … ” “Yes, because realestate.com is such a reliable source of information,” Dixson quipped. Before their terse exchange drew to a close, Simon called on the mayor to share where she lived or how much her house was worth, to which she responded curtly: “I don’t own a house.” Simon has since criticised Dixson for accessing his private address through a form he submitted to the council, and said it was a “gotcha moment” aimed at “launching personal attacks on speakers” if they did not agree with her views on the state government’s housing plan. “I’ve spoken at councils dozens of times over the last few years, and I’ve never had anything like this happen before,” he said. “How can people have confidence signing up to speak at Woollahra Council knowing that this is how their information is handled? This kind of privacy violation will have a chilling effect on community participation.”

Advertisement

Related Article Planning ‘It’s like a village’: What Woollahra residents really think about 10,000 new homes To register to speak at public forums, members of the public fill out a form and provide their full name, address, phone number and email address. Speakers must agree to a condition that states their face, voice and personal information will be recorded and publicly accessible on the council’s website. Asked why she accessed Simon’s address, Dixson said: “It’s publicly available information and was relevant to proving that claims made by the speaker were simply incorrect. “The vast majority of people who attended the meeting were there for all the right reasons.”

Dixson did not respond when asked if she had breached the code of conduct or searched for the addresses of any other speakers, and she did not confirm if she accessed Simon’s details independently or through a council staff member. Simon said the mayor’s action strayed far from debate about public policy and was an attempt to turn the conversation personal. “It potentially is a way to discourage participation from your opponents,” he said. “It reflects the weakness of her position that she feels the need to fall back on that.” Simon said he would submit a complaint to the Office of Local Government. Under Woollahra Council’s code of conduct policy, which sets the minimum standards of behaviour, integrity and performance expected, councillors must “only access council information needed for council business, and not use that council information for private purposes”. Academic Andy Asquith, who researches governance matters in local councils, said the behaviour benchmarks had vague wording and therefore made it unclear whether the mayor had breached the policy.

“It’s not a level playing field – you expect everyone is playing by the same rules … That sort of information is operational and should be accessed by a very small number of council employees, so the fact that the mayor accessed it is where the issue lies,” Asquith said. title: Nine Australians die of breast cancer every day. So why do we underestimate the disease?
text:

LifestyleHealth & wellnessBreast cancer Nine Australians die of breast cancer every day. So why do we underestimate the disease? Shona Hendley Updated October 1, 2026 — 3:07pm ,first published 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before 33-year-old Chontaine Adair was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic breast cancer in 2025, she had a very different perception of the disease. “I just didn’t think it could happen at my age, and I had a mindset that it couldn’t happen to me,” says Adair, who is based in Sydney. Chontaine and Landis Adair with their daughters Paisley, 7, and Xanthie, 6. Wolter Peeters This misconception, says the mother of two, was partly shaped by age-specific cancer-screening advice. “I didn’t know anyone in their early thirties with breast cancer, and any ads regarding checks like mammograms, for example, show older women and even mention, ‘If you are [a certain] age, get tested’, and this age was always older. They were not directed to younger women,” Adair explains. A new survey, funded by the National Breast Cancer Foundation (NBCF) as part of their Breast Cancer Awareness Month campaign, Unfinished Stories, has revealed that, as in Adair’s case, there is a disconnect between public perception and the reality of breast cancer today.

Advertisement

The survey, completed by 1003 respondents, found that 64 per cent underestimated the number of people diagnosed each year, 84 per cent underestimated the likelihood of recurrence and spread, and 51 per cent underestimated the number of Australians who die from breast cancer each day. Related Article Lunch with A little over half of women accept a free mammogram. Cassandra’s rare form of breast cancer wouldn’t have been detected without it Additionally, it found that nearly two-thirds (64 per cent) now see breast cancer as more manageable than other cancers, and over half (53 per cent) believe treatment advances have fundamentally altered public perceptions of the disease. Dr Cleola Anderiesz, chief executive of the NBCF, believes these findings reflect progress achieved through decades of research, including reducing Australia’s breast cancer death rate by more than 40 per cent over the past three decades, but also highlight a perception gap. “Research has transformed breast cancer outcomes. Yet breast cancer remains one of our most significant health challenges,” she says.

Advertisement

“The biggest gaps we’re seeing are around the scale and ongoing impact of breast cancer. Many people underestimate how many people are diagnosed each year [approximately 20,000], how likely breast cancer is to return or spread, and how many lives are still lost to the disease every day [approximately nine].” Specialist breast cancer surgeon Dr Chantel Thornton, who was not involved in the research, says that from her experience and among her patient cohort – predominantly premenopausal women – it’s very uncommon for them not to take the diagnosis seriously, but that some do underestimate the disease. Underestimating the seriousness of breast cancer can lead to decreased urgency around breast changes, say experts. iStock “Patients may underestimate the fact that breast cancer can metastasise to other organs, and therefore it is harder to treat them for a cure,” she says. Additionally, Thornton says some “people don’t understand that all breast cancers are not the same and different subtypes can infer different survival”.

Advertisement

A lack of understanding, or incorrect perception, can pose a range of risks at the individual level. “When people underestimate the seriousness of breast cancer, they may also underestimate the importance of breast awareness, screening and seeking medical advice about breast changes,” says Anderiesz. Loading It can also have a much broader effect, particularly in supporting ongoing research into the disease. Breast cancer still remains the second leading cause of cancer death in Australian women, says Professor Belinda Parker, NBCF-funded researcher at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre.

Advertisement

“Breast cancer is not just one disease; it changes. Everyone has their own individual cancer, and so some people have a type of cancer that has a very poor survival rate, and we can’t forget about those women.” Related Article Breast cancer The common breast cancer myth that might be putting women at risk Parker says continued investment in research is critical to build on the progress made and to investigate other areas of breast cancer that haven’t received as much attention. “We haven’t really made a big dent in women who get metastatic cancer, so when their cancer has spread to other sites … we also haven’t really made a big difference for treating diseases that have spread to the bone,” she says. “What we really need to do is focus on either preventing the deadly types of breast cancer or being able to target them head-on, and that’s where research is critical.”

Advertisement

Now, nearly a year after Adair’s diagnosis, following radiation and ongoing hormone-targeted treatment, her mindset and perception of breast cancer have changed. “I know now that it can happen to anyone at any age, and I now know breast cancer looks different for everyone, and that different types require different treatments.” Another key takeaway for Adair is that she now recognises the benefits of cancer research firsthand. “My targeted therapy is the result of research, and hopefully more treatment options will be developed by research in the future to help me give me time to watch my girls grow up, and others live long, healthier lives.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. title: An office chat about ‘Wharfie Time’ upset a colleague. What went wrong?

BusinessWorkplaceAsk an expert Opinion An office chat about ‘Wharfie Time’ upset a colleague. What went wrong? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor October 1, 2026 — 3:00pm

October 1, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I returned to work after the long weekend in Melbourne and the office was buzzing with chatter about the AFL Grand Final. I am not a footy fan, so usually don’t really participate in such discussions, but I had been invited to a grand final party and watched the game this year. I have to admit it was very exciting. Unfortunately, I seem to have made a bad mistake on the Monday after. I innocently asked what “Wharfie Time” was, something I hadn’t got a grasp of on the day. A colleague replied with words along the lines of: “It was a disaster – that’s what it was”. Then another colleague who wasn’t part of the conversation, but was within earshot, became very upset. We haven’t seen them since. What did I accidentally bring about? A colleague who wasn’t part of the conversation, but was within earshot, became very upset. John Shakespeare The person who became upset and fled the scene was unquestionably a Fremantle supporter. The Fremantle Dockers are the AFL’s second Western Australian team. They joined the league in 1995. Unlike their larger cousins, the West Coast Eagles, who joined in 1987 and had won the premiership (finished the champions of the entire competition) within six years, the Dockers have never reached that pinnacle. Saturday’s game was their best chance to break their drought. They had finished on top of the ladder at the end of the home and away season (the part of the football calendar that precedes finals) and at times looked invincible.

Advertisement

The grand final was a brilliant, close-fought game, but with less than five minutes to go in the last quarter, it looked like Fremantle had repeated a pattern that had defined their season: they had weathered the best football their opponent could muster and had accelerated towards victory. In short: never underestimate the power of football to affect people’s emotions. This is where Wharfie Time comes in. What you saw on the telecast was a kind of in-game celebration (I’ve seen it referred to as an “activation”, a term that makes me want to gag). I’d call it a crowd provocation in the form of a strange assortment of in-jokes and homages. Until the grand final, it had only happened twice before. Only this season. And only at Fremantle’s home ground in Perth. Fremantle sought permission from the AFL to use it at the grand final (under the right circumstances), and the AFL reportedly encouraged it. “Wharfie” is the Australian term for a dockworker, a name originally considered by the club administrators as the football club’s nickname, but sidestepped due to perceived political connotations. In 2009, however, the Dockers’ captain, Matthew Pavlich, addressed the playing group before a match while wearing a mic and implored his team to “Put on your superman capes, boys! It’s wharfie time!” (They lost the game comfortably.)

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Job hunting Why your closest friends probably won’t help you find a job Tim Duggan Work columnist The whole thing starts with a baleful funeral toll, taken directly from the AC/DC song Hells Bells. In Perth, the lights go out at this point, and it’s here that the similarity to the entrance of The Undertaker in WWE wrestling is impossible to ignore. In this way, it’s not just “sports entertainment,” it’s a pastiche of sports entertainment. A reference on top of a reference on top of a reference. While DNG! DNG! DNG! echoes through the arena, the words “WHARFIE TIME” appear on the stadium screen and the crowd goes berserk. This all happened, with the exception of the lights, at the MCG on Saturday afternoon. A bit of fun? Maybe. Hindsight is a wonderful thing, but I would certainly say it was ill-advised in a grand final against a team notorious for never being beaten. In a game where the gods can be so capricious, never tempt fate. Immediately after this iteration of Wharfie Time, Brisbane commenced one of the greatest (and probably the fastest) comebacks in grand final history, kicking an almost unimaginably brilliant four goals in four minutes. After the game, numerous Brisbane players referred to the gimmick as a catalyst for their late surge.

Advertisement

So that’s the potted history. Let’s address the question of what you accidentally brought about? Football trauma, plain and simple. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Is it a good idea to mix business with pleasure? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor And this is the problem of office footy chat. It’s a great tradition – in Melbourne, certainly, and I’m sure throughout Australia. But for those not versed in the intricacies and earnestness of a certain kind of deep supporterdom (and for those who are, but have never truly fallen in love with a club), a stray word or off-hand comment on a Monday morning can cause great pain. This wasn’t your fault. It probably wasn’t even the fault of your blunt colleague – although surely if they knew there was a Dockers supporter nearby they could have been a touch more tactful. But it does highlight the fact that a thing undertaken in fun – whether that’s a water cooler chat about a weekend event or a premature celebration of a seemingly certain victory – can easily go sideways. In short: never underestimate the power of football to affect people’s emotions.

Augustus Minerals has defined at least two higher-grade gold shoots at its Music Well project in Western Australia’s prolific Leonora-Laverton gold district, with both remaining open along strike. The interpretation comes from a combination of recent diamond and reverse circulation (RC) drilling, assays and soil sampling. Augustus says its geological detective work has stitched together data from drilling and surface geochemistry to outline a western shoot defined by soil samples over 400 metres of strike and an eastern zone defined by pathfinder geochemistry over 300m. Both are open to the north-northeast at the company’s Clifton East prospect. Augustus Minerals’ reverse circulation drilling at its Music Well project in WA’s gold-rich Leonora-Laverton gold district. The interpretation links together a string of solid, earlier RC drill hits, including 11m at 2.41 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 32m, 8m at 3.27g/t gold from 72m and 34m at 0.83g/t gold from 38m. Pathfinder elements in soil samples, including tellurium, bismuth, molybdenum and tungsten, have helped trace the orientation of the mineralised structures.

Advertisement

‘Pathfinder geochemistry indicates a similar strike for the strong intersection seen in an RC drillhole within the eastern shoot.’ Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford A recent diamond drill hole put in by Augustus appears to have provided the final piece of the puzzle. While assays from the hole returned only lower-grade gold anomalism, including 6m at 0.31g/t gold from 79m, 5m at 0.43g/t gold from 106m and 12m at 0.22g/t gold from 117m, management believes the results are significant. According to Augustus, the core revealed tell-tale alteration from hematite to silica-sericite-pyrite-carbonate, which strengthened closer to the gold-bearing part of the system, suggesting the hole may have passed along the edge of a bigger mineralised zone. Crucially, structural measurements from the diamond core indicate that the higher-grade quartz-pyrite (iron sulphide) veins dip steeply to the southeast, providing a clear target for follow-up drilling. Armed with this new structural understanding, the company drilled a series of northwest-oriented RC holes to test for higher-density veining between the original drill holes. Assays from that program are pending and expected in mid to late October.

Advertisement

In addition to the two defined shoots, the company has its eye on a third target, a 200-metre-long zone of anomalous rock chip and soil pathfinder results. With rock chips grading up to 1.8g/t gold, the anomalism coincides with a major fault in the east of the Clifton East prospect. The company says this area has not yet been drill tested. Augustus Minerals general manager exploration Andrew Ford said: “Integration of surface geochemistry, RC and Diamond drilling data has outlined two higher-grade shoots within the broader alteration system that are open to the north-northeast.” The company’s Music Well project covers a commanding 1242 square kilometres of exploration tenure just 35km north of Leonora, a town that sits at the heart of a storied gold belt with a total endowment of more than 28 million ounces. Augustus’ ground abuts tenements held by regional giants Northern Star Resources and Genesis Minerals, with major gold projects in the neighbourhood including Darlot, King of the Hills and Thunderbox. The definition of coherent mineralised shoots comes at a time when the region is a hive of corporate activity. The Leonora–Laverton gold district is in the middle of a broader WA gold consolidation wave, with majors on the hunt for new ounces to feed their processing hubs. That backdrop helps explain why fresh exploration success in the area is attracting attention, with regional gold assets and land positions in the district increasingly in focus. Recent activity includes the eye-watering $12.6 billion Genesis-Vault merger in July and Brightstar Resources’ September acquisition of five critical exploration licences from Panther Metals immediately adjacent to its developing Laverton processing hub.

Advertisement

Of late, Genesis has been hoovering up gold ounces across Leonora and Laverton, building a formidable feed pipeline around its mills. It picked up Focus Minerals’ Laverton project to feed its restarted three-million-tonne-per-annum plant and splashed $639 million on Magnetic Resources to get exposure to the 2.24-million-ounce Lady Julie deposit in 2026. That buying spree followed a $600 million acquisition of St Barbara’s Leonora assets, including the Gwalia mine and mill, in 2023. With assays from its latest targeted RC drill campaign due shortly and drilling operations set to kick off once wet ground conditions improve, Augustus looks set to generate plenty of newsflow. In a part of the world where big miners are looking for their next meal, defining coherent, higher-grade gold shoots is one way for a junior to get a seat at the table. Eating outOutdoor dining A lingering hangover has lifted: Patrons can now stand and drink outside city pubs In a win for vertical drinkers, the City of Sydney has updated its outdoor dining guidelines, ahead of a $20 million reform to expand outdoor dining spaces. Erina Starkey October 1, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From today, patrons can now stand up with a drink outside pubs, restaurants and bars operating across the City of Sydney, scrapping a long-standing rule that prevented people drinking on the footpath without a table or shelf. The updated outdoor dining guideline are part of a wider push to make outdoor dining a permanent part of the city’s streets. This change affects all City of Sydney suburbs, from St Peters to Potts Point, Elizabeth Bay, Erskineville and the CBD. Removing the lingering hangover from the guidelines means punters can wait on the footpath with a glass of wine until their table is ready, and stand out the front of the pub drinking a beer, provided the venue has a designated outdoor dining area. The idea is that the change will add energy and life to public spaces, bringing Sydney closer to the outdoor dining and drinking culture of many European cities. Locals drink on the street outside the Forrester’s in Surry Hills. Matt Johnson, group beverage director at Applejack Group, which runs venues across the City of Sydney council area, including Opera Bar, Surry Hills’ Forrester’s and The Butler in Potts Point, says the change will make a big difference to the group’s venues.

Advertisement

“It’s super exciting and just in time for summer too,” he said. “I’m from the UK, so I grew up in Brighton and London, where it’s completely the norm to be outside the pub standing with a pint, with friends. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “On our busier days, like Anzac Day and during the sports season, our pubs are bursting at the seams, so this will give us more space, and it creates such a good energy to be able to have guests standing and drinking outside.” Publican James Wirth said drinking outdoors was part of the experience at the Old Fitzroy Hotel in Woolloomooloo. “At The Old Fitz and our other pubs, the pavement pint is half the point, and people standing outside on a warm summer’s evening is what people come here for, and it creates a really vibe-y atmosphere outside.” The Forrester’s in Surry Hills. In practice, the no-standing rule has not really been policed said Councillor Jess Miller. “As far as I’m aware, it’s never really been enforced. To the best of my knowledge, council has never walked up to a person and said, ‘excuse me, you need to sit down or find some furniture’.”

Advertisement

Instead, venues have been largely policing themselves so as not to be in breach of their licensing conditions. “We would ask people to find a table, and it’s never really been a comfortable conversation,” said Johnson. “It never really made sense to us, especially when our guests are just there trying to enjoy themselves with a drink and there’s only so many tables available.” The Old Fitzroy Hotel in Woolloomooloo. Janie Barrett Wirth said the rule was never enforced at The Old Fitz, where people regularly drink on the pavement, but he still welcomes the change. “It’s a small change, but council deserves credit for making it,” he said. “It speaks to the fact that council is listening and respecting how people want to use these areas, and recognise that vertical drinking isn’t a safety problem.”

Advertisement

The change does not alter how alcohol is sold or served, which must still comply with each venue’s liquor licence. Patrons can’t wander off with their drink from the venue’s designated outdoor dining areas, and standing is allowed only within its approved outdoor footprint. A clear path must also remain for pedestrians, wheelchairs and prams. The Shakey in Sydney’s Surry Hills. Miller says the bigger story is about $20 million in reforms, due to roll out over the next eight years, to expand outdoor dining spaces across Sydney. Pop-up dining spaces, such as those in carparks or on-street areas currently bordered by concrete barriers, will be made permanent, and footpaths will be extended to allow more people to be seated outside.

Work is expected to begin in the next few months, with extended outdoor dining areas planned for Glebe, Redfern, Surry Hills, Newtown and Erskineville. “Adding paving and landscaping, and making [a] permanent area outside of restaurants can effectively double their capacity, and that will have a huge impact on business,” said Miller.

Thousands of doctors from the state’s major hospitals will walk off the job on Thursday afternoon as part of their ongoing dispute with the government over pay and working conditions. Doctors will gather outside Parliament House in Melbourne to call for improvements to their working conditions including, a 30 per cent pay rise over four years, a cap of 12½ hours on shifts, paid overtime, and a guarantee of three consecutive days off during a fortnight of work. Doctors will walk off the job at several major public hospitals across Melbourne next week. Gabrielle Charotte The four-hour industrial action follows more than a year of strained negotiations with the Victorian government. Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation president Dr Roderick McRae said this week that working hours and fatigue among doctors in hospitals are so severe, they felt they had no option but to strike again.

“Our doctors do not take the decision to go on strike lightly,” McRae said. Related Article Healthcare Doctors to walk off job at major Melbourne hospitals over pay dispute “But the reality is they are being rostered on for 84-hour weeks and frequently work even longer when emergencies occur. They are often completely exhausted and burnt out, with little opportunity to rest between shifts. The threat that this systemic fatigue presents to patient safety is simply unacceptable.” Emergency departments would be exempt from the strike, McRae said, and staffing would remain above Saturday levels to ensure patient safety would not be put at risk. McRae said despite more than 14 months of negotiations and more than 60 meetings with three health ministers, the state government had failed to address doctors’ concerns.

“The Victorian hospital system is in crisis, and everyday patient safety is under threat.” He said doctors had already undertaken four separate strikes in specific regional and metropolitan locations. “Over the last six months, the government has repeatedly promised doctors that ‘an offer was imminent’,” McRae said. “But despite this, we’ve seen absolutely nothing put forward.” Non-critical and elective surgeries are expected to be delayed as a result of the mass walkout on Thursday afternoon. title: Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet
text:
Advertisement

BusinessConsumer affairsPayments Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet Jessica Yun October 1, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Consumers and businesses are wrapping their heads around the Reserve Bank’s ban on card payment surcharges today and figuring out how it works. From October 1, you should no longer see an additional charge applied to card payments. If your coffee costs $5, that’s what you should expect to pay – at least, in theory. Card surcharges have been banned from October 1 onwards. Here’s what you need to know. Laurent Delhourme In practice, you may well still see a surcharge on your purchases as merchants and retailers adjust their approach. Here’s a quick cheat sheet on how the ban will work.

Advertisement

What has changed today? The Reserve Bank has changed the rules to now allow card networks – Mastercard, Visa and Eftpos – to ban surcharges for credit, debit and prepaid card payments made in store, online or via mobile wallets. PayPal, American Express, UnionPay are also removing surcharges from October 1. It means merchants are no longer allowed to charge an extra fee when you tap or insert your card at the point of sales, so the prices you see should be the price you pay. Retailers must clearly display how much an item or service costs with any applicable surcharge; so if you’re buying a $5 coffee, the displayed price should look like “$5.05 with card surcharge”. They must also disable surcharging on their terminals and take down any payment surcharge notices on display.

Advertisement

Behind the scenes, the new regime lowers processing costs for merchants by capping “interchange fees” – the fees paid between banks every time the customer taps or swipes their bank card. That fee goes from 0.8 per cent to a flat 0.3 per cent on Australian consumer credit cards. On domestic debit and prepaid cards, the ceiling has fallen from 10¢, or 0.2 per cent, to 8¢ or 0.16 per cent. Related Article Payments ‘Quite ill-prepared’: Shops scramble to meet new card surcharge ban What if I’m still being charged? Payment providers and banks have disabled the surcharge function on the terminals they control, but some older terminal machines don’t automatically update and may not yet reflect the changes. The RBA and the banking industry have urged patience as some businesses make the transition. Some business leaders have warned that some communities may not know about or understand the changes, particularly small business owners of migrant backgrounds or those who don’t speak English as a first language. The surcharge ban doesn’t include weekend and public holiday surcharges, which are still permitted.

Advertisement

Will businesses raise their prices? The short answer is: quite likely. These payment costs haven’t disappeared; they are just no longer allowed to appear as a separate charge. Most businesses are already facing and absorbing higher costs and overheads on many fronts and don’t feel able to absorb any more, so many will consider adjusting product or service prices and find savings elsewhere. How do I dispute surcharges? The ACCC and RBA can’t help you here – card networks (Visa, Mastercard and Eftpos) and payment providers (Square, Tyro, Stripe and some banks) – are in charge of enforcing the surcharge ban and will be held responsible if surcharges continue.

Advertisement

In the first instance, ask the merchant or retailer to clarify the surcharged amount (before payment if possible). Request a refund on the surcharged amount if necessary, and if they refuse, the next step is to report any unauthorised surcharges to your bank or card provider. The ACCC and state consumer protection agencies, such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria, will still be monitoring and enforcing consumer law to make sure businesses don’t mislead customers about prices or reasons for price rises. Should I pay in cash? The consumer watchdog has stated businesses are indeed allowed to offer discounts for a preferred payment method such as cash or PayID. “Payment method discounts should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay,” the ACCC states on its website.

Advertisement

We may well might start seeing more businesses, especially smaller ones, shifting back to cash as a result. According to Cash Welcome campaign manager Jason Bryce, this is already happening. Related Article Exclusive

Credit cards Surcharge ban could end popular free travel insurance perk “Most small retailers will raise prices to cover card costs and many will offer discounts for cash payments,” he said. So if you’re keen to save your dollars, keep some notes and coins on you. Will banks find a way to pass on the lost revenue? They already have, and not where you might expect to see it. Major banks have already wound back the generosity of credit card sign-on bonuses and rewards points earning rates, which were being funded by the higher interchange fees, and raising annual fees.

Advertisement

Commonwealth Bank has overhauled its loyalty program that pushes customers to spend rewards with Virgin’s Velocity scheme instead of Qantas Frequent Flyer points, and CBA customers who bundle multiple products, such as a mortgage or term deposits, will earn more points than those who have one account. Westpac has also announced fee hikes and cuts to benefits such as free travel insurance on its credit card line-up. NAB has made a number of changes that impact MyCard credit card holders (formerly Citibank cards) most dramatically; its premium “Prestige” card – which included 15 airport lounge visits, free hotel stay extensions and cashback on ride-shares, on top of generous points earning rates – has been scrapped entirely. American Express has also announced a scaling back of its airport lounge benefits. I’m a business owner. What should I do? It’s your responsibility to make sure you don’t continue to apply surcharges from today onwards. Get in touch with your bank or payment provider to implement the changes and update pricing details where you need to.

Advertisement

Shop around for the best deal. Corporate spending platform Archa’s chief executive Oliver Kidd recommends asking your card provider these questions: Has my points earn rate changed?

Have I lost any complimentary insurance?

Has my interest-free period changed?

Has my interest rate increased?

What am I really paying on foreign exchange fees, including any new mark-ups?

Has my credit limit changed without me knowing? “Business owners shouldn’t assume their card still offers the same value it did a year ago,” he said. If you’re looking more information, self-regulating body Australian Payments Network (AusPayNet) has put together an FAQ for consumers, businesses and payment providers at cardsurcharge.com.au. The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.
